title: Build your backend. Keep control.
text:
Build your backend. Keep control.

QB Flex gives your application a PGlite database, an authorized REST API, authentication, realtime events and object storage. Studio manages these services; your application connects through a publishable key and its own user sessions.

 Start here

1. Follow [installation](/docs/getting-started/installation).
2. Create your first project and an ownership policy.
3. Choose the [React tutorial](/docs/sdk/react/quickstart) or [Vanilla JavaScript tutorial](/docs/sdk/vanilla/quickstart).

 Three applications, one platform

Studio is the authenticated workspace for project developers. API owns management and application endpoints. Docs is this independently deployable documentation site. A background worker requests scheduled maintenance through an authenticated internal endpoint.

An organization owns projects. Each project owns an isolated primary branch. A branch has a separate PGlite directory and authentication realm. Organization roles and application user identities are different permissions.

 What is available

The implementation covers ordinary-table REST CRUD, application policies, password auth with browser passkey/TOTP adapters, row subscriptions, S3-compatible storage and encrypted backup/restore. Read [what changed](/docs/getting-started/updates), the [expanded-release status](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release) and [compatibility](/docs/reference/compatibility) before deployment. Experimental foundations are not complete delivery/native/WASM services.

GraphQL, vector search, functions, hosted MCP, general branching and replicas are roadmap capabilities. They are not required to use the core backend.

 Secure by default

A publishable key identifies a project. It does not grant access to rows. Tables remain private until exposed, and exposed tables still need applicable permissive policies. Platform credentials never become application user sessions.

title: What changed in QB Flex
text:
What changed in QB Flex

 Product 0.1.0 · specification 1.1

This documents the current development checkout, not a new product version or a declaration that the expanded release is complete. Start with the linked guides for usable workflows.

| Change | Status and guide |
| --- | --- |
| Dark-first console, light theme, mobile drawer, command palette and shared shadcn/Tailwind styling | Implemented [Studio workflows](/docs/studio/workspaces). |
| Schema workflow canvas and table detail sheet | Implemented [Schema Visualizer](/docs/studio/schema-visualizer). |
| Automatic refresh after Studio submissions | Successful forms refresh active views and mark inactive views stale; file transfers share the same behavior. [Studio workflows](/docs/studio/workspacesautomatic-refresh-after-submissions). |
| Platform/application passkeys and TOTP | Implemented browser/server adapters; deployment origins and physical ceremonies need verification. [Passkeys and MFA](/docs/authentication/passkeys-mfa). |
| Resend and React Email templates, optional SMTP adapter | Implemented [email configuration](/docs/authentication/email); live provider delivery requires deployment checks. |
| External S3-compatible storage, including operator-managed RustFS | Bundled MinIO removed. [Storage](/docs/storage/files) and [deployment](/docs/self-hosting/deployment). |
| Private streaming uploads with optional SHA-256 | Implemented application/management paths; resumable transfers remain planned. [Upload lifecycle](/docs/storage/files). |
| Streamed authenticated branch/control archive v2 and legacy restore | Implemented for both archive types; offline control recovery retains key/session revocation. [Backups](/docs/self-hosting/backups). |
| Synthetic policy SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE rehearsal | Implemented isolated real-engine simulation. [Policies](/docs/database/policies). |
| Conditional DELETE with expected revision | Implemented alongside PATCH; legacy calls unchanged. [REST](/docs/database/rest). |
| Encrypted durable jobs and Studio Job Inbox | Experimental foundation. [Job Inbox](/docs/studio/job-inbox). |
| Checkpointed, scoped database webhooks | Experimental signed delivery with policy revalidation, rotation, retries and SSRF-safe HTTPS. [Webhooks](/docs/studio/webhooks). |
| Security Advisor | Experimental metadata findings and expiring evidence-bound acknowledgments. [Advisor](/docs/studio/security-advisor). |
| Redacted Deployment Doctor and private latency histograms | Implemented foundations. [Doctor](/docs/self-hosting/doctor) and [monitoring](/docs/self-hosting/monitoring). |

 Expanded release is still in development

All twelve production/developer features, native/offline/background/push and four optional WASM integrations belong to the accepted expanded release. Foundations above do not satisfy the full objective. See [feature-by-feature status](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release), [native and push scope](/docs/roadmap/native-push), [WASM scope](/docs/roadmap/wasm) and the generated [specification 1.1](/docs/reference/development-spec).

 Documentation stays with the implementation

Contributions must update affected Docs guides, examples, configuration, availability and contextual Studio Help in the same change. API/SDK references and the specification mirror are generated from source. Search/navigation/sitemap metadata are regenerated and checked, and tutorial code is typechecked against the actual SDK. Run the documented repository gates before treating a changed workflow as available.

title: Install and run locally
text:
Install and run locally

 Requirements

Use pinned Bun 1.4.2. Native macOS development is the current development track; Windows uses WSL2/Docker, with native Windows execution experimental. A Docker-compatible engine is needed for optional Mailpit, bucket initialization and container verification. Object storage is separately supplied by you, such as RustFS; there is no bundled MinIO service.


bun install --frozen-lockfile
cp .env.example .env


Edit the new .env with your S3 endpoint/bucket/credentials and email provider selection. Do not commit it. Configure an endpoint reachable from the API process, then start native hot reload:


bun run dev


Studio runs on 7610, Docs on 7611 and API on 7612. The terminal startup panel confirms readiness and shows the service links; see [terminal logging](/docs/self-hosting/monitoringterminal-display) for display controls. Each app has independent workspace commands. Database files and generated local secrets live under ignored .data.

The launcher checks occupied ports and waits for the API to create/accept its worker credential. If the full Docker local profile owns these ports, use its running apps or stop those application services before hot reload:


docker compose --profile local stop studio docs api worker
bun run dev


This preserves database volumes and separately managed storage. Native .data and Docker's database volume are separate installations. A worker must use its API's QB_DATA_DIR or securely supplied QB_WORKER_TOKEN; never create/copy a token file to bypass startup checks.

 Object storage and email

Run RustFS or your chosen provider independently. For native development .env.example assumes an S3 endpoint at http://127.0.0.1:9000. [Storage configuration](/docs/storage/files) explains the remaining variables and container addressing.

For local SMTP inbox capture:


docker compose --profile dependencies up -d mailpit


Select QB_MAIL_PROVIDER=smtp, QB_SMTP_HOST=127.0.0.1 and QB_SMTP_PORT=7615 for native API development. Mailpit's inbox is on 7616. Alternatively configure [Resend and React Email](/docs/authentication/email); explicit SMTP selection overrides a present Resend key.

The optional storage-init service runs inside Docker, so use a container-reachable endpoint when invoking it:


QB_S3_ENDPOINT=http://host.docker.internal:9000 docker compose --profile dependencies run --rm --build storage-init


The service needs your configured bucket/credentials; provider provisioning failure is not a healthy storage configuration. Do not reuse example placeholders as real credentials.

 First owner

Open Studio's setup flow. A clean local installation stores the one-time token at .data/bootstrap.token; never commit it. Enter it with your name, email, password and organization. After setup the file is removed, Studio opens sign-in, and setup cannot create another owner. Passwords require at least 12 characters. Production requires injected master/bootstrap/worker secrets and administrator MFA.

 Verify your installation


bun run qb doctor --directory .
bun run check
bun run build


Doctor is redacted inventory, not a live provider certification. The optional bun run spike checks integration candidates but does not make GraphQL/vector product capabilities available. See [compatibility](/docs/reference/compatibility) and [production deployment](/docs/self-hosting/deployment).

title: Create your first project
text:
Create your first project

 Create a project

In Studio select your organization and create a project with a name and URL-safe slug. The initial region is local. Project creation returns an operation while the primary database is provisioned; Studio polls until the operation finishes.

Select the ready project. Its primary branch is shown with a production badge. Changes affect the selected branch.

 Create the task table

Use Database → Migrations to apply a migration:


CREATE TABLE tasks (
  id TEXT PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT (replace(gen_random_uuid()::text,'-','')),
  owner_id TEXT NOT NULL,
  title TEXT NOT NULL,
  completed INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (completed IN (0, 1)),
  revision INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1
);
CREATE INDEX tasks_owner_idx ON tasks(owner_id);


The schema is private at this point. In the exposure editor enable the table and allow its five columns, including the primary key.

 Add ownership policies

Create a policy for each of select, insert, update and delete, with the authenticated role and permissive mode. Both the read expression and write check use the same ownership condition:


{"op":"eq","left":{"column":"owner_id"},"right":{"claim":"sub"}}


This permits users to read and modify only their own tasks. An attempted ownership reassignment fails the write check and rolls back.

 Connect an application

Create a publishable key in API → Keys. Copy it when shown; only its hash and prefix are stored. Use the real project ID and primary branch alias in your client configuration. Run either example application with those values.

Sign up as an application user. This account is separate from your Studio owner. Insert a task with that user ID as owner_id, then open a second application account to confirm isolation.

 Generate types

The API workspace exposes generated types. The CLI writes the same declarations:


bun run qb types generate --project YOUR_PROJECT_ID --branch primary --output qb-flex.types.ts


Regenerate after schema changes. Runtime validation and authorization still apply to typed requests.

title: Build your first application
text:
Build your first application

 Prerequisites

Complete [installation](/docs/getting-started/installation) and [first project](/docs/getting-started/first-project). Create the tasks table with its generated ID, owner, title, completion flag and revision. Expose the columns and add owner checks for SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE. Create a publishable key.

 Choose a client track

Run bun run --cwd examples/react dev for the React application at port 7617, or bun run --cwd examples/vanilla dev for the DOM application at port 7618. Both implement the same workflow. Configure the API URL, project ID and publishable key in the form. Add that application's exact origin in Studio Authentication settings.

Follow the [React provider tutorial](/docs/sdk/react/quickstart) or [Vanilla JS tutorial](/docs/sdk/vanilla/quickstart). React uses a context provider, shared auth state and query/mutation hooks. Vanilla uses a client instance, DOM handlers and explicit cleanup.

 Register and create tasks

Register an application user with an email and a password of at least 12 characters. This account is separate from your Studio account. Add a task, mark it complete and delete it. The client sends the current user ID, and the API validates ownership independently.

Open a second browser profile with another application user. Each user should see only their own tasks. Attempting to update another user's ID returns a missing/invisible resource response.

 Receive changes

Both examples subscribe after loading a snapshot and its consistency token. Make a task change in another tab signed into the same user: the task list updates through committed, authorized events. Disconnect networking briefly, then restore it; the subscription resumes or requests a fresh snapshot when its retention window has expired.

 Add file attachments

Create a private bucket named attachments in Studio Storage. Enter its bucket ID in the example. Upload a file, download the exact bytes and delete it. Another user cannot list or download that private object. See [storage authorization](/docs/storage/files).

 Generate types and recover

Generate types in Studio API or with qb types generate. Create an encrypted backup, restore it into a separate branch and inspect the recovered task rows. Active sessions are excluded and object bytes need separate S3 backup. The primary branch changes only through an explicit cutover.

 Verify the workflow

The repository's browser checks run these workflows against the real API. Run QB_INTEGRATION_STORAGE=1 bun test tests/integration with an explicitly configured isolated S3-compatible backend and Mailpit ready, then bun run test:browser. SDK packages are built and packed locally; no registry release is performed.

title: Use QB Flex Studio
text:
Use QB Flex Studio

 Console navigation

Studio is a dark-first developer console built with shared Tailwind v4 tokens and shadcn/Radix primitives. Switch to the tokenized light theme using the theme control. Collapse the desktop sidebar or open the mobile menu; sidebar/theme choices persist locally. Docs shares tokens but keeps its documentation layout.

Organization, project and branch selectors define the target. Check the environment before SQL, migrations, credential changes or restore. Overview displays real project/schema state, service shortcuts and recorded activity—not simulated traffic or a complete Operations Dashboard.

Press Command-K (macOS) or Ctrl-K to search navigation/projects. Outside text entry/dialogs, use g then o for Overview, w Workspace, d Database, s Schema, a Authentication, l Activity or t Settings. Keyboard focus, Escape-to-close dialogs/sheets and reduced-motion styling remain important; exercise critical workflows on your own devices.

 Sign-in and protected routes

Studio verifies the platform cookie session before loading a protected workspace. Password, authenticator and passkey sign-in all confirm that the browser can read its session before announcing success. A protected direct link returns to the same local path after sign-in; external URLs and authentication loops are rejected. Session checks bypass HTTP caches, use bounded requests and revalidate on navigation, window focus and once a minute while a workspace is open. API errors display Connection unavailable with a retry action instead of redirecting to sign-in.

For local development, Studio aligns an API configured as localhost or 127.0.0.1 with the browser's corresponding loopback hostname so HttpOnly cookies remain same-site. Remote API hosts retain their configured URL. Passkeys still require their enrolled RP hostname and browser support; changing hostname does not migrate a passkey. If cookies cannot be established, sign-in reports that condition and remains on the form. Keep production origins, HTTPS and cookie settings consistent. These route guards improve navigation; API authorization remains authoritative.

First-owner setup creates the owner and then opens sign-in. It does not treat a setup response as a browser session. Signing out cancels pending reads and clears identity-specific cached data. Reload and browser history must recheck the session before rendering protected content.

 Workspace onboarding and lifecycle

When no workspace is selected, Studio shows a full-page onboarding view to choose an existing workspace or create a first workspace. Empty selection is intentional: switching workspace clears the current organization and returns to that screen. Workspaces are organizations in the model, so profile changes and archive/delete act at that workspace level.

 Workspace details

Open Workspace in the sidebar (/workspace) to manage the selected organization. A workspace has its own profile image, shown in the workspace selector and on the details page. Owners and admins can rename the workspace and upload a cropped PNG, JPEG, or WebP avatar (up to 1.5 MB).

Archive hides a workspace from normal selection while retaining its projects and data. Restore from onboarding’s archived list or from workspace details. Deleting a workspace is owner-only and requires typing the workspace name. Deletion removes only that workspace’s project databases, project-scoped storage objects, function trees, API keys, secrets, backup rows/files, audit records and job targets. Other workspaces and their objects remain untouched. There is no automatic offline archive of workspace bytes during delete, so keep existing backups where you need recovery.

 Workspace map

| Workspace | Route | What is available |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overview | /overview | Project summary and service/activity shortcuts. |
| Workspace | /workspace | Workspace profile, avatar, projects, archive and delete. |
| Database | /database | Table creation, schema/data, policies, privileged SQL and migrations. |
| Schema | /schema | [Workflow-canvas visualization](/docs/studio/schema-visualizer) and detail sheet. |
| Authentication | /auth | Branch users, session administration and provider configuration. |
| API | /api | Endpoint/keys/type information. |
| Realtime | /realtime | Current subscription semantics/capabilities, not full trace debugger. |
| Storage | /storage | Logical buckets and authenticated upload/download/delete. |
| Backups | /backups | Snapshot and isolated restore with explicit cutover workflow. |
| Activity | /logs | Audited actions; the route remains backward compatible. |
| Job Inbox | /jobs | Experimental [job metadata/history/cancel/replay](/docs/studio/job-inbox). |
| Webhooks | /webhooks | Experimental [scoped signed database deliveries](/docs/studio/webhooks). |
| Security | /security | Experimental [Advisor findings and acknowledgments](/docs/studio/security-advisor). |
| Settings | /settings | Account/security, organization membership, and Project settings (identity, quotas, delete). |
| Functions; AI & Vectors | /functions; /ai | Planned-state screens, not executable services. |

Setup and sign-in are outside the authenticated shell (/setup, /sign-in). The development port remains 7610. No /notifications or Data Lab workspace is available yet.

 Database workflow

Select a table; use New table to configure columns/keys/defaults/constraints and review generated SQL before creation. Creation defaults private, with a separate explicit exposure toggle; policies must still be configured. Read bounded grid pages, server-filter/sort, choose visible columns, edit typed values/nulls and export the current page. JSON array imports are atomic and capped at 100 rows. Presentation column toggles do not change public exposure. Studio database privileges are organization permissions, not an application identity.

Migrations record immutable IDs/checksums and use the existing audited/backup path. Configure exposure and separate read/write policies; use the legacy simulated-identity read tester. Advanced isolated fixture write tests are available through the [policy-test endpoint](/docs/database/policies), not a complete Advisor UI.

 Authentication, profile and secrets

Manage branch users and revoke sessions with authorized roles. Provider settings include Google/GitHub credentials, exact origins and verification. Secret values are encrypted and are not returned by configuration reads.

Account settings provide profile/security controls, avatar upload/cropping, password changes, TOTP and platform passkey management. Avatar storage requires configured S3. Use [passkeys/MFA](/docs/authentication/passkeys-mfa) and [administrator recovery](/docs/authentication/administrator-mfa); platform identity never proves application access.

 Project settings

Open Settings → Project for the selected project. This tab is project-scoped; workspace (organization) profile, archive, and delete live under Workspace (/workspace).

An organization administrator can rename the project and save its region. Slug and status stay fixed after creation. This release stores the region as local and runs the project on this node. Saving another region is rejected and does not move databases, storage, or authentication. Quotas for database size, reserved object storage, and request rate are edited on the same tab. The project list, overview, and shell refresh after a successful save.

 Delete project

Delete project permanently removes only that project: branch databases, function trees, storage objects under its prefixes, keys, secrets, backups, and project-scoped catalog and audit rows. Sibling projects and the workspace remain. Confirm by typing the project slug. After deletion, Studio clears the project selection and refreshes lists. Workspace-level deletion under Workspace removes the organization and every project it owns; prefer project delete when you intend to keep the workspace.

 Safe operations and errors

 Automatic refresh after submissions

Successful Studio mutation forms automatically refresh active lists, counters, selectors and details before their success callbacks finish. This includes row creation/edit/delete/import, schema/configuration changes, credentials, profile/avatar changes and Job Inbox, webhook and Advisor actions. File uploads/deletions and project/authenticator setup use the same refresh helper after the server acknowledges completion. You do not need to reload the page manually.

Older in-flight reads are cancelled before refreshing so they cannot overwrite post-submission data. Inactive cached workspaces are marked stale and fetch again when opened; disabled queries wait until enabled. Failed submissions do not trigger this refresh or clear existing data. If a subsequent read fails, the acknowledged write is still successful: investigate the read error rather than submit the write again. This is Studio behavior, not a promise that arbitrary SDK applications automatically update their own caches.

Async writes surface success/error feedback; loading skeletons and empty states do not imply an operation succeeded. Destructive controls use explicit confirmations. Audit entries contain actor/action/resource rather than raw credentials or protected rows. Diagnose unavailable branches using [monitoring](/docs/self-hosting/monitoring), and restore through the [backup runbook](/docs/self-hosting/backups).

App-user realtime tests must use that application's identity. Management access is not proof of policy authorization. Functions, AI, general branching, previews, notifications and advanced operations remain accurately marked [planned or incomplete](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release).

title: Schema Visualizer
text:
Schema Visualizer

 Open the selected branch

Choose the organization, project and branch in the console, then open Schema (/schema). The approvals-ui-derived workflow canvas uses React Flow to display the branch's schema. It is an inspection tool; moving a node does not change the database.

 Read the graph

Each table card shows its name, column count, types and primary-key markers. Exposure badges distinguish private from exposed tables. Foreign-key edges point to referenced tables. Private tables are still visible to authorized Studio operators; this does not make their rows publicly readable.

Use the legend, minimap, fit and zoom controls to explore the graph. Select a table to inspect all columns, nullability, indexes, exposure/allowed columns and policies in the detail sheet. A table being exposed does not establish a permissive policy grant.

 Keyboard and smaller screens

Tab to a table and use Enter or Space to open details. Escape closes the sheet. Visible focus indicators and labeled controls support keyboard navigation. On small screens use the console's mobile menu and pan/zoom controls rather than relying on hover. Animation respects reduced-motion preferences.

Loading, empty and failed schema requests have separate states. If there are no tables, create one in Database; if a request fails, verify project access and branch availability before retrying.

 What this page does not do

It does not apply migrations, approve schema changes or rehearse them locally. The expanded Schema Change Review and SQLite WASM rehearsal are not implemented. Apply reviewed changes through [schema and migrations](/docs/database/schema); test public access with [policies](/docs/database/policies).

title: Job Inbox
text:
Job Inbox

 Experimental foundation

Open Job Inbox (/jobs) for the selected project and branch. Durable jobs are experimental. [Database webhooks](/docs/studio/webhooks) now have checkpointed producers and an authenticated executor; alert emails, recovery drills and push campaigns remain separate pending integrations. An empty inbox does not mean these integrations are available.

The queue stores encrypted payloads in private branch tables under the existing single writable owner. Studio and management clients receive metadata only: kind, state, timestamps, attempts and safe error codes. Payloads, secrets and lease credentials are not shown.

Skipped webhook jobs can finish as succeeded with a controlled skip code. Inspect lastCode/history: PROVIDER_ACCEPTED means receiver handoff, while NOT_AUTHORIZED, KEY_REVOKED, SUBSCRIPTION_INACTIVE and EVENT_EXPIRED mean nothing was dispatched. Queue success is not proof of user delivery/reading.

 States and attempts

| State | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| queued | Waiting for its eligible time and an executor. |
| leased | Claimed for a bounded lease with a fencing token. |
| retry_wait | Failed/expired attempt awaiting another bounded attempt. |
| succeeded | Executor recorded success; not proof of downstream delivery/read. |
| dead | Retry/deadline budget exhausted or payload unusable. |
| cancelled | Future claims/completions are fenced. |

The list refreshes every 15 seconds and supports bounded pagination. Select a job for attempt history; Escape closes the dialog. Viewers can inspect metadata. Administrator-authorized cancel/replay operations are audited and require explicit confirmation in Studio.

 Cancel or replay

Cancellation cannot undo an external side effect already sent by an executor. Reconcile uncertain outcomes before retrying. Dead-letter replay creates a new job with the original event ID and a parent-job link. It is explicit, not an infinite automatic retry.

Replay requires Idempotency-Key; keep the same key when retrying an uncertain replay request. A new deliberate replay needs a new key. Push replay is blocked until recipient-aware campaign retry exists. Webhook receivers must deduplicate event IDs. Replays recheck current projection/authorization and require the source event to remain inside the 24-hour outbox window.

 Management client and routes

Trusted management code can use ManagementClient.jobs(projectId, branchId).list, get, cancel and replay. Keep management tokens server-side; Studio can use its platform cookie. The helpers retain the standard { data, meta } envelope.

| Method | Branch-relative route | Access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | /jobs?limit=100&cursor=… | Viewer or higher; maximum 500 rows. |
| GET | /jobs/{id} | Viewer or higher; includes attempt history. |
| POST | /jobs/{id}/cancel | Administrator-authorized audited write. |
| POST | /jobs/{id}/replay | Administrator-authorized audited write; idempotency key required. |

Prefix routes with /management/v1/projects/{projectId}/branches/{branchId}. Cursors bind the route, actor and immutable branch. Do not reuse them after switching users or targets. There is no public submission API yet.

 Resource and executor boundaries

Payloads are limited to 64 KiB; a branch permits at most 10,000 pending jobs. Leases default to 30 seconds and cannot exceed 60 seconds. Scheduled eligibility is bounded to seven days. Terminal history/deduplication is retained for 30 days; cleanup does not erase pending work.

Kind policies bound webhook/email attempts to ten within 24 hours, push to six within one hour, and maintenance/drills to three within 24 hours. These are queue policies, not certification of those integrations.

Private internal claim/finish endpoints require immutable project/branch IDs and derive allowed kinds from the executor credential. The webhook executor selects a server-defined subset and cannot consume other work. QB_WORKER_TOKEN cannot claim push work. QB_PUSH_ENABLED=false is the default; enabling its separate QB_PUSH_WORKER_TOKEN only enables a restricted principal, not a push worker or notification service. Keep /internal/ off the public gateway. See [expanded release status](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release).

title: Durable webhooks
Security Advisor
text:
Security Advisor

 Experimental metadata diagnostics

Open Security (/security) for the selected project/branch. Run a scan to review severity, resource, evidence and remediation. The Advisor samples no production rows, issues no application tokens and makes no policy/exposure repairs. A clean report is not proof of security. Static checks supplement the actual [policy simulator](/docs/database/policies), not a second authorization engine.

 Findings

| Code | Interpretation |
| --- | --- |
| MISSING_GRANT | No enabled permissive grant for an exposed operation. Access fails closed; this is informational, not an authorization bypass. |
| UNREACHABLE_GRANT | All permissive grants contain a literal false access/check condition. Verify intended access in the simulator. |
| SENSITIVE_COLUMN_EXPOSURE | Exposed column names resemble passwords, secrets, tokens, private keys or credentials. A naming heuristic, not inspection of their contents. |
| BROAD_ANONYMOUS_GRANT | An unconditional anonymous permissive policy needs review. Additional restrictive policies reduce severity but require actual simulation. |
| PUBLIC_BUCKET | A public-read bucket exposes bytes intentionally; verify that this is appropriate. |
| AGING_CREDENTIAL | An active project credential has a known creation age of at least 90 days. |
| CREDENTIAL_AGE_UNKNOWN | Legacy creation provenance is missing. Unknown is not fresh. |
| CREDENTIAL_SCAN_LIMIT | The bounded credential inventory is incomplete. |
| ADMIN_MFA_GAP | Organization owner/admin accounts lack TOTP; evidence is an aggregate count, not email addresses or secrets. |

Key creation times live in additive control metadata and are backfilled only from existing creation audits. Their age survives later audit retention. Expired/revoked project credentials are excluded. The scan does not currently inventory all platform management tokens; live provider diagnostics and a complete security audit remain outside these static checks.

 Acknowledge, do not hide risk

Administrator-authorized acknowledgment writes are audited and expire within 30 days. Studio offers one/seven/30 days with explicit confirmation; administrators can clear them early. Finding IDs bind code, severity, resource and evidence. Changed evidence does not inherit an old acknowledgment. Stale/resolved IDs return FINDING_STALE; refresh before retrying.

Acknowledged findings stay visible; the dashboard separates them from unacknowledged counts. Exact expiry makes the risk unacknowledged again. Acknowledgment cannot weaken policies, enable public access or disable the existing administrator MFA gate. Isolated branch restore drops acknowledgments so restored state requires fresh review.

 Limits and authorization

Scans examine up to 100 tables, 500 public buckets and 500 active project keys, return up to 500 findings and explicitly mark truncation. Evidence uses schema/configuration metadata; it never contains row values, token hashes, raw keys or provider responses. At most 500 unexpired acknowledgments are stored per branch. Policy relationship/type/constraint certification and hard simulation execution budgets remain expanded-release acceptance work.

Management reads require viewer access within the project; acknowledgments require administrator-authorized audited writes and existing MFA enforcement. Application sessions, publishable/service keys and unrelated project credentials do not authorize this surface. Organization administrator MFA evidence is limited to the selected project's organization. There are no public simulation-token or automatic-remediation endpoints.

 API and repository management client

Prefix with /management/v1/projects/{projectId}/branches/{branchId}:

| Method | Route | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GET | /security | { scannedAt, schemaVersion, findings, truncated, limitations }. |
| POST | /security/{findingId}/acknowledge | { expiresAt } in Unix milliseconds, future and no later than 30 days. |
| DELETE | /security/{findingId}/acknowledge | Clear an acknowledgment; idempotent. |

ManagementClient.security(projectId, branchId).scan/acknowledge/clear retains the standard response envelope and cancellation support. Keep management credentials server-side. Operational alert email/webhook delivery is still a separate pending integration; findings are not automatically sent externally.

title: Schema and migrations
text:
Schema and migrations

 Supported objects

The generated REST API supports ordinary tables with stable primary keys. Composite keys use a base64url-encoded JSON array in primary-key order. Views, virtual tables and custom-trigger tables are not automatically exposed.

PGlite provides embedded PostgreSQL. Studio and new migrations use PostgreSQL SQL. Studio SQL is a privileged developer operation. Reserved _qb_ objects, extensions, filesystem access, role/configuration changes and explicit transaction control are blocked through the console.

 Exposure

New tables are private. Exposure chooses the allowed public columns; all primary-key columns must be included. Policies are a separate requirement. Hiding a column rejects projections, sorting and filtering against that column.

 Migration lifecycle

Each migration records its identifier, checksum, author and application time. Reapplying the same identifier and content is idempotent. Changing the content of an applied migration returns a conflict.

Apply migrations under the branch owner transaction. Destructive migrations trigger a consistent backup first. Failed SQL or foreign-key validation rolls back the schema changes. Successful changes advance the schema version and regenerate managed event triggers.

Use forward migrations for corrections. There is no automatic destructive rollback. Restore a backup into an isolated branch when data recovery is necessary.

 Representation

REST/SDK booleans remain 0/1, including native PostgreSQL BOOLEAN columns. TIMESTAMPTZ values return UTC ISO strings; JSON/JSONB values return JSON text. Legacy converted text timestamps and JSON retain their original representation. PostgreSQL integer, BIGINT, BYTEA and identity columns are supported. Integers outside JavaScript's safe range are returned as strings. Write these values as signed 64-bit decimal strings. Blob writes and equality filters use canonical base64; JSON columns require valid JSON text. Blob values are base64 encoded in row responses and in authorized realtime projections.

 Generated types

Types describe the exposed schema, nullable values, defaults and generated columns. Simple CHECK (column IN (...)) constraints on literal values generate enum unions. More complex constraint expressions require explicit application validation. Insert fields with defaults are optional; generated fields are read-only. Keep declarations under version control and regenerate when migrations change.

 Out-of-band schema changes

The branch records a fingerprint of user tables, indexes, views and triggers. A schema changed through direct file access returns SCHEMA_STALE on public reads, mutations, schema discovery and row subscriptions. Reconcile it with a reviewed forward migration through Studio or CLI. Trusted file access still bypasses application row policies.

 Visual creation and inspection

Database's New table dialog configures columns, supported types, keys, defaults, nullability and supported constraints/foreign keys, with SQL preview before applying through the migration path. Creation defaults private; the dialog has an explicit exposure toggle. Exposing a table does not grant row access—add policies separately. The [Schema Visualizer](/docs/studio/schema-visualizer) inspects the topology and detail sheet; it does not apply migrations. Destructive Schema Change Review, approval binding and WASM rehearsal remain [expanded requirements](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release).

 Convert an existing SQLite installation

Use the offline [engine migration workflow](/docs/self-hosting/engine-migration). SQLite SQL is not accepted by the new engine. Applied migration SQL and checksums remain historical evidence; create new forward migrations using PostgreSQL SQL.

title: Write and test access policies
text:
Write and test access policies

The experimental [Security Advisor](/docs/studio/security-advisor) highlights missing/unreachable grants and risky exposure. Its findings never replace the actual policy-test engine or automatically change grants. [Webhook subscriptions](/docs/studio/webhooks) also revalidate current SELECT policies and column projections before dispatch.

 Policy model

QB Flex implements row policies in its application layer. Direct filesystem access to PGlite is trusted access and bypasses these checks. Policies are restricted JSON expressions rather than arbitrary SQL or JavaScript.

An operation needs at least one applicable permissive grant. Matching permissive expressions are ORed, and restrictive expressions are ANDed. No applicable grant means denial.

 Ownership example

For a table with owner_id, compare the column to the server-supplied authenticated subject:


{"op":"eq","left":{"column":"owner_id"},"right":{"claim":"sub"}}


Create separate select, insert, update and delete policies. Include authenticated in the role list for all signed-in users, or a custom [application role](/docs/authentication/roles) name for narrower grants. A policy matches when its role list intersects the credential class (anonymous / authenticated / service) or the user's assigned custom roles. For inserts and updates use the ownership expression as the write check as well.

 Available expressions

Boolean expressions support and, or, not, true and false. Comparisons support eq, ne, lt, lte, gt, gte, in and isNull. Operands reference validated columns, verified sub/role claims or scalar values.

Relationship-existence expressions support {"op":"exists","relationship":"APPROVED_NAME","where":{"op":"true"}} for registered, exposed relationships. They apply the related table's select policies as well as the where expression. Unapproved relationships, cycles and excessive nesting are rejected. See [relationships and reviewed RPC](/docs/database/relationships-rpc) for setup and limits.

 Read and write semantics

Reads apply policies before counts and pagination. Updates check both the old row and the actual updated row; an ownership change cannot escape the new-row check. Atomic batches roll back if any prospective row is denied. Returned rows require select permission.

 Test identities

Use Studio's policy tester with a simulated user ID and role (system or custom). It executes the policy-filtered query without creating an unrestricted token. Then verify with real application users: two users should see separate rows, counts and realtime events.

 Realtime permissions

Events are reevaluated with current identity and policy. A deletion or row leaving visibility delivers only its key to an identity that could read the old image. A user who could not read that row receives no event.

 Isolated synthetic write simulation

Developer-authorized POST /management/v1/projects/PROJECT_ID/branches/BRANCH_ID/policies/test accepts operation (select, insert, update, delete), table, synthetic identity, optional fixtures mapping table names to row arrays, query, mutation input, row key and revision. Only explicitly supplied fixtures enter an ephemeral in-memory database; production rows, sessions and jobs do not. The real engine evaluates exposure, old-row access and prospective-row checks; scratch writes never commit to production.

The response's data contains allowed, oldRowAccess, prospectiveRowCheck, result rows and optional error. Null checks mean not applicable/not reached, not a grant. Returned rows still require select access. Owner bounds:100tables/1,000fixture rows/1MiB total input; the HTTP JSON limit remains64KiB. This simulator does not prove unsupported/custom schemas safe and does not mint user tokens.

Requests without operation or fixtures keep the previous policy-filtered read response. Service/privileged request flags never bypass policies. Security Advisor scans/acknowledgments are a separate expanded requirement not yet available.

 Try an ownership-change rejection

As a developer with management authorization, POST this JSON to the existing policy-test endpoint after creating/exposing tasks with ownership SELECT/UPDATE policies and a prospective ownership check:


{
  "table": "tasks",
  "operation": "update",
  "identity": { "sub": "alice", "role": "authenticated" },
  "fixtures": {
    "tasks": [{ "id": "fixture-task", "owner_id": "alice", "title": "Synthetic", "completed": 0 }]
  },
  "key": "fixture-task",
  "input": { "owner_id": "bob" }
}


With those policies, old-row access passes but the prospective row fails. Inspect data.allowed, data.oldRowAccess, data.prospectiveRowCheck and the safe error; never infer a grant from a null check. Repeat with a valid update and another synthetic subject. Fixtures must satisfy the real table constraints, including required/default columns and foreign keys. This request uses no production row contents and creates no application session.

Studio's existing identity tester uses the legacy filtered-read path. Advanced write simulation currently uses the management endpoint; a dedicated Advisor UI is not present.

title: Query the REST API
text:
Query the REST API

 Endpoints

The branch base URL is:


/v1/projects/{projectId}/branches/{branchId}


Use the primary alias or an explicit branch ID. Include X-QB-Key with a publishable key. Include an application bearer token when authenticated.

 Structured reads


{"columns":["id","title"],"filters":[{"column":"completed","op":"eq","value":0}],"order":[{"column":"id","direction":"asc"}],"limit":50,"count":true}


POST this body to /data/tasks/query. The default page is 50 rows; maximum is 500. Filters never accept raw SQL. Counts include only authorized rows.

 Pagination

Follow the response's meta.cursor with the same projection, filters, ordering, identity and schema version. Cursors are signed and bind that query scope. Changing scope rejects the cursor. Pagination does not provide a database snapshot spanning multiple requests.

 Writes

POST inserts one row or an atomic batch of up to 100 rows. PATCH updates a row by key; DELETE removes it. Supply Idempotency-Key to safely reconcile a retried mutation. Reusing the same key with different content returns a conflict.

Tables with a server-managed revision column support conditional PATCH and DELETE through If-Match. The server increments revisions on updates and rejects stale values with CONFLICT (HTTP 409). Existing calls without a revision remain compatible; do not treat a stale write as an automatic retry.


await client.from('tasks').update(task.id, { title }, { revision: task.revision });
await client.from('tasks').delete(task.id, { revision: task.revision });


These are alternative mutations against a freshly read row, not a sequence using the same revision: after an update, refetch the current revision before deleting.

 Results and errors

Success returns data and meta, including a request ID and relevant schema metadata. Errors provide a stable code, human-readable message and retryability. SDK methods throw QBError on failed responses.

An invisible row is returned as unavailable without revealing whether it exists. Public responses do not contain SQL, filesystem paths or credentials.

title: Relationships, upsert and reviewed RPC
text:
Relationships, upsert and reviewed RPC

 Register a relationship

Create a foreign key with a migration, expose both tables and the linking columns, then PUT a declaration to the branch Management API /relationships. Specify name, source, target, localColumn, foreignColumn and cardinality (one or many). A one relationship must follow a source foreign key. Reverse foreign-key links can use many.

A related query must select its linking column. Use .include([{ name: 'project' }]) after registering that relationship. Child rows pass their own SELECT policies; an invisible parent becomes null, and an invisible child collection becomes empty. Counts still describe authorized parent rows. Nested expansion is unavailable.

 Existence policies

A policy can use an expression with op: 'exists', a registered relationship name and a where expression evaluated against the target table. The target's SELECT policies are also enforced. This cannot turn a hidden table into a public join. Cycles and relationship paths deeper than four levels are rejected.

 Upsert

.upsert(row, { idempotencyKey }) requires every primary-key field. An absent row follows INSERT/WITH CHECK; a conflict follows old-row UPDATE/USING and new-row WITH CHECK. The entire batch rolls back if one row fails. It does not grant access to invisible conflicts. Returned rows must pass SELECT policies.

 Reviewed named operations

Developers register a declaration by PUT to /rpc in the branch Management API. A declaration contains name, table, kind, typed args, optional query settings, and value mappings. Mutation kinds are insert, update or delete; update/delete require keyArg. A value mapping can use { arg: 'title' } or { claim: 'sub' }. Claims come from the server identity.

The browser calls qb.rpc('operation_name', args, options). This API exposes structured operations over the same read/mutation engine. SQL text, arbitrary functions and unrestricted transactions are unavailable. Generated RPC declarations describe argument and return types. Pass both generated interfaces to createClientDatabase, RPC(options) to check operation names, arguments and results.

title: Authenticate application users
text:
Authenticate application users

 Separate realms

Platform sessions authorize Studio and management operations. Application users belong to a branch's authentication realm. Tokens from another project or branch are rejected, even when the same email address exists in both.

Better Auth provides password hashing, session creation, verification, reset and OAuth mechanisms. QB Flex provides routing, realm isolation and reserved metadata tables.

 Email and password

Use SDK auth.signUp, auth.signIn and auth.signOut. Passwords require at least 12 characters. Auth requests are rate limited. Studio Authentication can also create users, edit profiles, assign [application roles](/docs/authentication/roles), block or delete users, and revoke sessions. Session revocation takes effect on later requests and realtime authorization checks.

 Verification and reset

Enable email verification in project settings and configure [Resend or SMTP](/docs/authentication/email). Both adapters render React Email templates. Unverified users cannot sign in when verification is required. SDK sendVerification requests a new message; resetPassword requests a reset link, and updatePassword completes it with the one-use token.

Use an allowlisted callback URL. Local SMTP messages can appear in Mailpit. Provider failures are surfaced, not silently treated as delivered messages; provider acceptance is not proof of inbox delivery.

 Google and GitHub

Register an OAuth application with the selected provider. Configure its callback to the explicit branch auth endpoint, then store its client ID and secret in project settings. Add the browser application origin to the project allowlist.

Call auth.signInWithProvider and navigate to the returned authorization URL. After the callback, refresh the application session. These adapters require provider credentials and live callback verification before certification.

 Browser sessions

The API uses HttpOnly cookies where supported, while SDK bearer tokens remain in memory. The client refreshes session state on initialization. Do not put service keys or management tokens in browser applications. Cross-origin cookies may be restricted by browser privacy settings; use a same-site deployment or explicitly manage an approved session adapter.

 Platform MFA

Platform owners can enable Better Auth two-factor authentication. Production readiness requires administrator enrollment and MFA enforcement; local availability alone is not a production certification.

 Passkeys and application TOTP

Browser clients expose auth.passkey enrollment/list/rename/remove/sign-in and auth.twoFactor enable/verify/disable. A password login requiring TOTP throws MFA_REQUIRED; complete the challenge and refresh the session before reading protected data. See [passkeys and MFA](/docs/authentication/passkeys-mfa) for origin restrictions, SDK examples and recovery cautions. Native ceremonies are not implemented yet.

title: Administrator MFA and recovery
text:
Administrator MFA and recovery

 Enroll the platform owner

Open Studio Settings even before creating a project. Enter the current password and enable the authenticator. Import the shown TOTP URI into an authenticator application, save the one-time recovery codes in a password manager and verify a code. The seed is shown during enrollment and never logged.

Production defaults to QB_REQUIRE_ADMIN_MFA=true. Owner and administrator writes require enrollment. Viewer access does not disclose secrets. Application user authentication is a separate branch realm.

 Sign in with MFA

After password verification, Studio shows the authenticator challenge. A password-only response does not contain an authenticated platform session. Enter a valid TOTP code to complete login. The Better Auth plugin applies attempt limits and locks repeated failed challenges.

Enrollment verification rotates the active session. Management tokens are revoked when enrolling; issue new project-scoped tokens after completing MFA. Keep recovery codes outside the data volume.

 Credential recovery

Use Better Auth's authenticated backup-code verification endpoint /platform/auth/two-factor/verify-backup-code when your authenticator is lost. Treat a recovery code like a password. An operator should revoke compromised management tokens and application sessions, rotate project keys and provider secrets, then examine audit events.

Never change the database's MFA columns to bypass a lost factor. Restore the protected control-plane backup only through an operator-reviewed recovery process.

 Passkeys are an additional method

Studio account settings also enroll, list, rename and delete platform passkeys. Its sign-in page offers Sign in with passkey. This does not turn off QB_REQUIRE_ADMIN_MFA or replace its TOTP enrollment requirement. Keep a usable recovery method and test the configured Studio RP hostname/origins. See [passkeys and application MFA](/docs/authentication/passkeys-mfa).

title: Subscribe to row changes
text:
Subscribe to row changes

 Commit-driven events

Managed triggers write events in the same transaction as row changes. Rolled-back writes produce no events. Events have branch-local IDs, schema versions and insert/update/delete operations.


const channel = qb.channel({
  table: 'tasks',
  onEvent(event) { console.log(event.event, event.payload); },
  onStatus(status) { console.log(status); },
}).subscribe();
// When the screen is removed:
channel.unsubscribe();


 Snapshot and cursor

A query result contains meta.consistencyToken. Pass that value as the subscription cursor to receive changes committed after the snapshot boundary. Reconnect resumes from the last processed cursor and deduplicates event IDs.

Treat events as invalidation signals when maintaining a filtered/paginated list. Refetch the authorized query rather than assuming every update still belongs in your current list.

 Authorization

Join validates the publishable key, branch, session and exposed table. The connection rechecks authorization while delivering events. Session expiry, revocation or key removal closes the connection. Changes to identity reset the subscription.

Only authorized columns are delivered. Row removals deliver permitted keys. Do not treat realtime as a way around read policies.

 Delivery limits

The implementation provides single-node branch ordering and at-least-once replay. Frames are bounded to 64 KiB. Heartbeats keep connections active. Slow clients are disconnected rather than accumulating unlimited buffers.

Presence, broadcast, binary channels and multi-node fan-out are planned capabilities. Persistent application messages belong in ordinary authorized tables.

 Debugger status

Connection callbacks, reconnect/replay and resynchronization behavior are available in the client. A dedicated Realtime Debugger with bounded metadata traces, replay-gap/latency diagnostics and scoped application debug sessions is still required by specification 1.1. Studio management privileges must not masquerade as a user's authorization proof. Do not record protected payloads or credential-bearing URLs when diagnosing your application.

title: Passkeys and application MFA
Resend and React Email
text:
Resend and React Email

 Shared authentication mail

Platform and application verification/password-reset messages render the repository's React Email templates. Both Resend and SMTP send HTML plus a plain-text link. These are authentication messages, not a bulk mail or operational-alert service.

 Resend configuration

Set these server-only values before starting the API:


QB_MAIL_PROVIDER=resend
QB_RESEND_API_KEY=replace_with_provider_api_key
QB_MAIL_FROM=QB Flex hello@example.com


Use a sender authorized by your provider and test verification/reset on your deployment. Keep the API key out of browser VITE_ configuration, Studio screenshots and source control. Templates live in packages/auth/src/email/templates.tsx; there is no Studio template editor yet.

 Provider selection

| Setting | Behavior |
| --- | --- |
| QB_MAIL_PROVIDER=resend | Requires QB_RESEND_API_KEY; explicitly chooses Resend. |
| QB_MAIL_PROVIDER=smtp | Uses the SMTP relay even when a Resend key is present. |
| QB_MAIL_PROVIDER=auto or omitted | Chooses Resend when its key exists, otherwise SMTP. |

SMTP is an alternative adapter, not automatic failover after a failed Resend send. Delivery errors are surfaced; configuration presence or a provider's acceptance does not prove inbox delivery.

 SMTP and local Mailpit


QB_MAIL_PROVIDER=smtp
QB_SMTP_HOST=127.0.0.1
QB_SMTP_PORT=7615
QB_SMTP_SECURE=false
QB_MAIL_FROM=QB Flex hello@localhost


These host/port values are for native development with Compose Mailpit. Containers use mailpit:1025. Set QB_SMTP_USER and QB_SMTP_PASSWORD only if the relay requires authentication. QB_SMTP_SECURE=true selects implicit TLS; configure the port to match your relay. Mailpit's local inbox is http://localhost:7616.

Production requires the selected provider's configuration. Never assume production mail works because local Mailpit passed. Enable project verification settings and use allowlisted callback URLs. See [application authentication](/docs/authentication/overview) and [Deployment Doctor](/docs/self-hosting/doctor) for lifecycle and redacted inventory checks.

title: Upload and download files
Application roles
text:
Application roles

 Scope

Application roles belong to a branch authentication realm. They are not platform organization roles (owner / admin / developer / viewer). Studio Authentication → Roles manages named roles; Authentication → Users assigns them.

System policy roles remain anonymous, authenticated, and service. Those names are reserved and cannot be created as custom roles.

 Simple named roles

Each role has a lowercase slug (^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,62}$) and an optional description. Users may hold many roles. There is no permission matrix in Studio—authorization is expressed through Database policies that list role names.

 Identity claims

Signed-in application users resolve to:

- role: always authenticated (credential class)
- roles: string array of assigned custom role names

Anonymous and service identities use empty roles. Banned users do not establish an application session identity.

 Policies

A policy applies when Policy.roles intersects { identity.role } ∪ identity.roles. Example: a policy with roles: ["editor"] grants only users assigned editor. A policy with roles: ["authenticated"] still matches every signed-in user, including those with custom roles.

Create or edit policies in Studio Database, selecting system or custom roles. Policy tests can simulate a custom role alongside a subject ID.

 Studio administration

Organization admin (or higher) can:

- Create, edit, block, unblock, and delete application users
- Assign roles and revoke sessions
- Create, rename, and delete roles

Blocked users have sessions revoked and cannot authenticate until unblocked.

title: Client SDKs
text:
Client SDKs

The two SDK packages share the same transport, authentication and authorization semantics. Choose the React package for component-level state and caching, or the framework-independent package for direct calls.

| Application | Packages | Guide |
| --- | --- | --- |
| React 19 | @qb-flex/client, @qb-flex/react | [React quickstart](/docs/sdk/react/quickstart) |
| Vanilla JavaScript | @qb-flex/client | [JavaScript quickstart](/docs/sdk/vanilla/quickstart) |

 Package availability

SDK artifacts are built and packed locally. They are not yet published to the npm registry. Workspace examples import the local packages. External applications can install the generated tarballs from dist/packages.


bun run sdk:pack


 Client configuration

Provide an API URL, project ID, branch alias/ID and publishable key. Set an exact application origin in project settings. Create one browser client for the application. SSR applications must create a separate client and query cache per request.

 Error handling

Methods return successful data envelopes and throw QBError for failures. Inspect its code, status and retryable fields. Validation, policy denials and conflicts should be corrected by the application; repeatedly retrying them does not help.

 Shared lifecycle

Subscriptions expose explicit cleanup. Session refresh is single-flight. Safe reads and explicitly idempotent writes receive bounded retries. Requests support timeout and AbortSignal cancellation.

React Native, encrypted offline writes, background tasks and Expo push are accepted expanded-release requirements but not implemented. See [native/push scope](/docs/roadmap/native-push). GraphQL, functions and AI remain deferred product candidates. Browser React and JavaScript are the current implemented client tracks.

 Newly added client capabilities

The shared client supports [browser passkeys and application TOTP](/docs/authentication/passkeys-mfa), conditional PATCH/DELETE revisions, cancellation and [optional upload checksums](/docs/storage/files). Generated [JavaScript declarations](/docs/reference/vanilla-api) and [React declarations](/docs/reference/react-api) remain the precise signatures; there is no published native package or push helper to install yet.
