Vanilla JavaScript quickstart
text:
Vanilla JavaScript quickstart

 Vite application

The runnable example is in examples/vanilla. It uses ordinary DOM APIs and no React dependency.


bun run --cwd examples/vanilla dev


Set the API URL, project ID and publishable key in the example configuration form. Add http://localhost:7618 to the project's exact origin allowlist.

 Import and initialize


import { createClient } from '@qb-flex/client';
const qb = createClient({
  url: 'http://localhost:7612',
  projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
  branch: 'primary',
  publishableKey: 'YOUR_PUBLISHABLE_KEY',
});


Install the locally packed client artifact when integrating into a separate Vite application.

First run bun run sdk:pack in QB Flex. In your Vite application, install the resulting tarball using its actual absolute path:


npm install /path/to/QBFlex/dist/packages/qb-flex-client-0.1.0.tgz


Import the client in your application entry module. The repository example already supplies a complete Vite configuration and can be copied as a starting application; its Vite version is pinned to 8.3.2.

 Direct browser modules

The Docs build includes a standalone browser ESM bundle at /sdk/client.js. Copy it into your application's public directory and import it locally:


script type="module"
  import { createClient } from '/sdk/client.js';
  const qb = createClient({
    url: 'http://localhost:7612',
    projectId: 'YOUR_PROJECT_ID',
    publishableKey: 'YOUR_PUBLISHABLE_KEY',
  });
/script


Serve the page over HTTP; do not open it through a filesystem URL. The standalone client bundle has no React or Node runtime dependency.

 Run the tutorial

Prepare the [task table and policies](/docs/getting-started/first-project), then add [authentication and CRUD](/docs/sdk/vanilla/data) and [realtime/file workflows](/docs/sdk/vanilla/realtime-storage).

title: JavaScript authentication and CRUD
JavaScript realtime and files
Use the qb CLI
text:
Use the qb CLI

 Login and linking


bun run qb login --url http://localhost:7612 --email owner@example.com
bun run qb projects list
bun run qb link --project YOUR_PROJECT_ID --branch primary


On macOS, login reads the password from a hidden interactive prompt and stores a 30-day management token in the OS keychain. Add --organization ORGANIZATION_ID only when the CLI must provision projects. Linux and CI use QB_MANAGEMENT_TOKEN: create the scoped token in Studio Settings after completing administrator MFA and inject it through your protected environment store. The CLI does not print or write credentials to a plaintext configuration file.

 Schema workflows


bun run qb db migrate --file migrations/001_tasks.sql --id 001_tasks
bun run qb db export --table tasks --output tasks.json
bun run qb db import --table tasks --file tasks.json
bun run qb types generate --output qb-flex.types.ts


Migrations and table writes require developer permissions. Import uses bounded batches; an import spanning batches is not a single all-or-nothing transaction.

 Recovery


bun run qb backup create
bun run qb backup restore --backup YOUR_BACKUP_ID


Restore creates a new isolated branch. It does not switch primary traffic automatically. Perform cutover deliberately through management operations after validating the restored branch.

 Development

qb init writes a local configuration file without credentials. qb dev starts the workspace processes. Commands accept explicit project/branch flags, with linked defaults for convenience.

General branch creation, functions, hosted MCP and remote reset are not enabled in P0. Unsupported commands return an actionable error rather than simulating success.

 Local reset and secrets

qb db reset --data-dir .data --confirm-local-reset requires a stopped API and a disposable local directory with a generated master key. It removes the local databases and generated local keys. It never selects a remote branch by default.

qb secrets set --name SERVICE_SECRET --env MY_SECRET reads a secret from the named environment variable, stores an encrypted version and returns only its identifier. Viewer access cannot recover secret values.

qb storage sync --bucket BUCKET_ID --directory ./attachments adds missing objects from a local directory. Existing and remote-only objects are preserved. Hidden files and symlinks are skipped. Use the explicit object APIs for deletion.

qb db diff --file expected-schema.json compares the current introspected schema with your checked-in schema manifest. It reports column differences; it does not invent a migration.

 Deployment Doctor

bun run qb doctor --directory . reports structured, redacted readonly inventory. No implicit network probes, writes, email or push. Use --probe-url https://your-api.example.com for an explicit bounded readiness GET; values and paths remain redacted. Exit0 means no blocking inventory errors,1 means errors,2 means invalid invocation. Unknown provider/native/recovery checks are not reported as healthy.

See the [Deployment Doctor guide](/docs/self-hosting/doctor) for exact probe restrictions, findings and limitations. Preview environments, push campaign tools and advanced recovery commands are not available simply because specification 1.1 defines them.

 Offline control catalog backups

With the API stopped, qb backup control-create --data-dir DIRECTORY writes a streamed encrypted v2 control archive. qb backup control-restore --data-dir DIRECTORY --file ARCHIVE --confirm-local-control-restore accepts new and legacy control archives, verifies them and replaces the stopped catalog only after an encrypted rollback checkpoint. Preserve all referenced branch files and the original master key. Restored sessions/credentials do not revive; reissue project/management keys. Both commands wait for streams and hold exclusive volume ownership. See [control recovery and limits](/docs/self-hosting/backupsstreamed-offline-control-recovery).

qb db migrate-engine --from sqlite --to pglite --data-dir SOURCE --output-dir DESTINATION --check reports compatibility. Omit --check to create and validate a separate PGlite installation while preserving the source. Stop writers first; see [engine migration](/docs/self-hosting/engine-migration).

title: Deploy a single node
text:
Deploy a single node

 Deployment shape

The self-host Compose overlay runs Caddy, API/database owners, maintenance worker, Studio, Docs and one-shot storage-init. Object bytes live in your separately operated S3-compatible provider, such as RustFS. There is no bundled MinIO service or object-storage volume. Mailpit belongs to local development, not production mail.

Keep writable PGlite directories on persistent local disk with one API volume owner. Do not start multiple writers against the same volume or put live databases on network filesystems.

 Prepare domains and secrets

Use a Linux AMD64/ARM64 Docker Engine host and Compose v2. Resolve API, Studio and Docs DNS to the host, and expose only gateway ports 80/443 publicly. Copy .env.production.example to a protected, untracked .env and replace placeholders.

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| QB_API_DOMAIN, QB_STUDIO_DOMAIN, QB_DOCS_DOMAIN | Domains used by the overlay/gateway and public URL configuration. |
| QB_APP_ORIGINS | Exact additional browser origins; no wildcard. |
| QB_MASTER_KEY | Encryption custody; preserve independently offline. |
| QB_BOOTSTRAP_TOKEN | One-time first-owner setup. |
| QB_WORKER_TOKEN | Private maintenance and metrics credential. |
| QB_S3_ENDPOINT, QB_S3_REGION, QB_S3_BUCKET | Reachable object-provider endpoint and physical bucket. |
| QB_S3_ACCESS_KEY, QB_S3_SECRET_KEY | Server-only object-provider credentials. |
| QB_RESEND_API_KEY, QB_MAIL_FROM | Resend authentication-mail configuration. |

Generate independent secrets locally, for example with openssl rand -hex 32. Never put them in images, source control, browser variables or documentation. Losing the original master key prevents decrypting protected settings/archives. The overlay enables QB_REQUIRE_ADMIN_MFA=true and derives production HTTPS URLs from domains. Runtime QB_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is distinct from the overlay's QB_APP_ORIGINS input.

[Email configuration](/docs/authentication/email) covers explicit QB_MAIL_PROVIDER and the SMTP alternative (QB_SMTP_HOST, port, user/password and TLS). Provider configuration does not certify delivery.

 External RustFS or other S3 storage

Use an endpoint reachable from containers, not their own 127.0.0.1. For a host-local provider, use http://host.docker.internal:9000; the current Compose includes the Linux host-gateway mapping. Remote production providers should use HTTPS.

The one-shot initializer tries HeadBucket/CreateBucket. Operators can provision the bucket independently when bucket-creation rights are unavailable. Inspect initializer output and verify upload/download on your actual backend. Its failure does not prevent API boot and must not be mistaken for a successful storage setup.

 Build and start


docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.selfhost.yml --profile selfhost config --quiet
docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.selfhost.yml --profile selfhost build
docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.selfhost.yml --profile selfhost up -d
docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.selfhost.yml --profile selfhost ps


Avoid printing the fully expanded Compose configuration because it may contain secrets. Caddy obtains TLS certificates; check DNS/firewall if issuance fails. Verify public /ready and Studio/Docs over HTTPS, then inspect bucket provisioning:


curl -fsS https://api.example.com/ready
docker compose -f compose.yml -f compose.selfhost.yml --profile selfhost logs --tail 100 storage-init


Production startup requires injected configuration, not an already-created owner. Open Studio to create the first owner using the bootstrap token, enroll/verify TOTP and securely save recovery codes. Remove the plaintext bootstrap token after setup; the API does not require it again once an owner exists. Platform credentials must never become browser application credentials.

 Day-two capacity and recovery

Upload staging reserves local disk before S3 PUT: plan for up to four 100 MiB uploads plus headroom, WALs and archives. Branch backup/restore streams share a two-operation capacity and 120-second deadline. Do not delete live WAL files or scale out writers to solve disk/queue pressure.

Monitor /ready, bounded logs and private /internal/metrics. The gateway blocks /internal/ with 404; scrape only on the trusted private network with the worker credential. [Deployment Doctor](/docs/self-hosting/doctor) adds redacted inventory and an optional explicit readiness probe, not automatic provider tests.

Protect three separate recovery assets: encrypted database/control snapshots, S3 object bytes/versioning and the original master key. [Branch restore](/docs/self-hosting/backups) creates an isolated branch; there is no automatic cutover. Sessions, provider tokens, jobs, webhook destinations and Advisor acknowledgments do not resume from a branch restore.

The existing worker runs experimental [database-webhook deliveries](/docs/studio/webhooks) through private APIs without PGlite writes. Default egress is public HTTPS only. Optional QB_WEBHOOK_INTERNAL_ALLOWLIST must match on API and worker; exact origins map to fixed reviewed IPs with TLS verification retained and known metadata destinations prohibited. [Security Advisor](/docs/studio/security-advisor) provides static operator findings, not automatic fixes or external alert dispatch.

 Upgrade and rollback

Create and verify a fresh backup before changing versions. Build the reviewed commit/digest and run the same up -d workflow. Named volumes persist. Never use down -v as an upgrade or port-change step. Validate schema compatibility before rolling code back; data rollback uses an isolated restore and explicit alias cutover, not a data merge.

 Docs publishing and verification

Set QB_DOCS_URL and VITE_DOCS_URL consistently before generation/build for correct sitemap/canonical links. Docs is independently deployable and needs no login; its production build prerenders content. Do not expose provider secrets to it.

Run repository checks/builds, CLI/browser checks and isolated test:compose/Linux gates for the affected boundaries. These do not replace production TLS, mail/OAuth/device/provider checks or sustained load/recovery evidence. Linux AMD64/ARM64 are certification targets; current evidence must be checked per architecture.

 Expanded features are not silently enabled

Keep QB_PUSH_ENABLED=false. A separately supplied distinct QB_PUSH_WORKER_TOKEN only enables a restricted queue principal in current source; it does not deploy a Node push executor or campaigns. Off-node Recovery Center, alert deliveries, advanced operations and native/push/WASM integrations remain [expanded-release work](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release).

 Existing SQLite data

The new API refuses a data directory containing control.sqlite. Run the [offline engine migration](/docs/self-hosting/engine-migration) into a separate directory, validate it, then schedule activation through QB_DATA_DIR. Keep the original installation and master key for recovery.

 PGlite owner memory

QB_MAX_BRANCH_OWNERS defaults to four and accepts 1–32. Each active branch has an independent PGlite WASM instance; the control catalog is additional. Size memory for the intended active branch count and snapshot export/import. On the local macOS ARM64/Bun 1.4.2 startup measurement, four empty branch owners including authentication reached about 2.7 GB process RSS, with roughly 0.9-second startup per owner. This short local measurement is not a production capacity guarantee; run bun scripts/pglite-benchmark.ts on the deployment host. The raw repository evidence is docs/benchmarks/pglite-macos-arm64.json.

The self-host Compose API memory ceiling defaults to 8 GiB (QB_API_MEMORY=8g) to leave room for the catalog, four branch instances and snapshot work. This is a configuration default, not measured Linux certification; lower the owner count or adjust memory only after measuring the deployment workload. The Compose environment passes QB_MAX_BRANCH_OWNERS to the API.

title: Backups and restore
text:
Backups and restore

 Consistent snapshots

Snapshots are created through the database owner using PGlite dumpDataDir(), then encrypted using AES-256-GCM and recorded with a checksum and schema version. Use the owner snapshot workflow; copying a live database directory is not a consistent backup.

Manual snapshots are available in Studio and the CLI. The maintenance worker requests scheduled backups. Retention is configurable; the default is seven days.

 Isolated restore

Restore decrypts and verifies the checksum, loads a snapshot into a new branch database and validates schema, constraints and manifest evidence. Active sessions, verification challenges and stored OAuth access/refresh tokens are excluded. Restored application users remain in the isolated database and must establish new sessions.

Validate expected table data, policies and migrations before cutover. The restored branch has its own authentication identity and routing.

 Production cutover

The cutover endpoint requires the project owner role and an explicit project-slug confirmation. It creates a rollback backup, closes the old primary owner and changes the primary alias. Existing requests and sockets must be reconciled against the changed branch.

The previous primary is retired and refuses public reads and writes. Restore the rollback snapshot into another isolated branch to reverse the cutover. Do not assume that alias switching merges data.

 Object bytes and control metadata

Branch snapshots do not back up S3 object bytes. The worker separately creates encrypted, checksummed control catalog snapshots under backups/control with the same daily/weekly retention. Protect the master key and copy archives off the node; configure object-store versioning/backups separately.

Control recovery is offline. Stop the API/worker, preserve all referenced project database files and verify the archive before replacement. The local ownership lock prevents restoration over a running API. The command checks integrity, foreign keys, applied control migrations and referenced branch files, creates an encrypted rollback checkpoint, excludes platform sessions and revokes all restored project/management credentials. Reissue keys after recovery.


bun run qb backup control-create --data-dir .data
bun run qb backup control-restore --data-dir .data --file CONTROL_ARCHIVE --confirm-local-control-restore


Inject the original QB_MASTER_KEY for production recovery. A catalog archive does not include project databases or object bytes; coordinate their recovery to a compatible checkpoint.

 Recovery drill

Create representative data, take a snapshot, alter the data, restore into another branch and compare results. Repeat after a process restart and verify secrets/session behavior. Publish measured RPO/RTO only after a reference-dataset drill passes.

 Retention and cancellation

Maintenance keeps the daily window (QB_BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS, default 7) and one newest checkpoint per week (QB_BACKUP_RETENTION_WEEKS, default 4). Preserve encrypted snapshots and the master key on separate storage for disaster recovery. A local backup volume is not off-site redundancy.

Project provisioning can be cancelled through POST /management/v1/operations/{id}/cancel while its status is requested. Running or completed operations return OPERATION_NOT_CANCELLABLE; cancellation never rolls back a committed database operation.

 Streaming branch archive v2 and compatibility

New branch archives use authenticated QBFARCH2 framing, AES-256-GCM and an incremental raw SHA-256 manifest digest. Encryption/decryption use bounded streams and private staging rather than reading the whole snapshot into memory. Authentication, expected size and checksum must pass before restored data is registered or exposed. Wrong keys, damaged headers/tags/bytes or digest mismatch fail with BACKUP_CORRUPT; failed partial files are cleaned up.

Legacy branch archives remain readable, including their original checksum semantics. Do not rewrite stored checksums by hand. The new format is not promised readable by older API versions; preserve a validated compatible restore runtime during upgrades. Control-catalog snapshots now also use streamed v2 framing with an authenticated control-kind marker, creation time and raw SHA-256 digest. Legacy encrypted JSON/base64 control archives remain readable through a bounded decoder.

Backup/restore shares a two-operation concurrency bound and a 120-second stream deadline. Archive validation has a size bound of at least 1 GiB or the configured database-write quota, whichever is larger. This is a bound, not a certified restore-time target. Snapshot schema version comes from the captured database, not a concurrently changed live branch.

Restores remove durable jobs as well as sessions/challenges/provider tokens. Neither old pending deliveries nor push registrations/campaigns should be revived. Object bytes and master-key custody remain separate responsibilities. Restart cleanup removes recognized abandoned temporary artifacts only under exclusive data-volume ownership; never manually sweep arbitrary live database files.

 Recovery Center status

Automated encrypted off-node destinations, freshness alerts, scheduled isolated restore drills and separate database/object/key reports remain required by specification 1.1. Today's manual restore is not the complete Recovery Center. The daily snapshot/seven-daily/four-weekly defaults and reference RPO 24 hours/RTO 60 minutes are planning defaults/measurement targets, not universal guarantees. See [expanded release status](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release).

 Streamed offline control recovery

qb backup control-create and control-restore keep their existing command names, data directory and explicit restore-confirmation flag. They wait for streams before returning. Create retains path and raw 64-character SHA-256 checksum, adding format: 2 and snapshot byte size. Restore retains its original result flags/rollback path and adds the source format.

New control archives authenticate kind, creation time, size, checksum and PGlite engine/version inside the v2 header. Physical datadir snapshots require the pinned compatible PGlite runtime. Legacy SQLite archives produced by QB Flex remain readable through the validated offline converter, which blocks incompatible schemas or values. Legacy archive envelopes remain readable without buffering their entire encrypted JSON/base64 envelope. Control archives are not interchangeable with branch archives, even with a matching key. The original master key remains mandatory and is never stored alongside archives.

Control snapshots permit one active write per catalog, default to a 1 GiB plaintext limit and have a 120-second streaming deadline. Disk checks budget private staging plus encryption/rollback headroom. Temporary directories use mode 0700 and plaintext/archive files use 0600. Authentication/checksum and native integrity/foreign-key/migration/dependency checks precede replacement. Missing branch files or bad archives fail without replacing the catalog.

Control recovery excludes platform sessions/challenges/provider tokens and revokes project/management credentials as before. Branch files and their identities are a separate recovery asset; coordinate compatible branch snapshots rather than assuming the control archive contains them. The replacement and its directory are fsynced, and an encrypted rollback is created before replacement. Only exact recognized abandoned control staging is removed under the exclusive volume lease; final archives and operator files are preserved. Graceful API shutdown waits for in-flight maintenance/control streams before closing the catalog and releasing ownership.

PGlite dumpDataDir(), integrity checks and checkpointing remain native synchronous operations. The streaming deadline/cancellation applies to hashing/encryption/decryption, not preemption of a running PGlite call. This is not an off-node Recovery Center or an automated drill/cutover service. New-format archives require a compatible restore runtime; older binaries are not guaranteed to read v2.

Engine conversion preserves live credentials and durable work in a stopped installation. Backup restoration has different semantics: it strips sessions, provider tokens, jobs and webhook subscriptions, and control recovery revokes credentials. See [engine migration](/docs/self-hosting/engine-migration).

title: Migrate SQLite to PGlite
text:
Migrate SQLite to PGlite

QB Flex now stores the control catalog and each project branch in persistent PGlite directories. Studio and new migrations use PostgreSQL SQL. REST/SDK booleans remain 0/1, binary values remain base64, JSON remains text, and unsafe integers remain decimal strings.

 Prepare and inspect

Stop the source API and maintenance worker. Preserve the original installation, master key and object-store backups. Do not point the new API at the SQLite directory: startup rejects it. Conversion requires both exclusive volume ownership and the legacy SQLite lock.


bun run qb db migrate-engine --from sqlite --to pglite --data-dir /srv/qb-sqlite --output-dir /srv/qb-pglite --check


The check inspects the control catalog and every referenced branch. Custom views/triggers, virtual/generated columns, unsupported defaults/constraints/indexes, mixed-type values and invalid constraints block conversion. SQLite input must use UTF-8; invalid UTF-8 and embedded NUL bytes in text are rejected rather than rewritten. Resolve reported blockers in a reviewed copy of the source before retrying. The converter never silently drops objects or coerces incompatible values. Checks can be slow because they inspect every value.

Source and destination must not overlap. Existing destination directories must be empty. Symlinks require manual review. Provide enough private disk and memory for PGlite initialization, conversion and snapshot export/import; archive limits do not guarantee available memory.

 Convert and validate

Run the same command without --check. The command creates control.pglite/ and projects/project/branches/branch/main.pglite/, preserving immutable IDs. It copies the existing keys and archive files, keeps historical SQL/checksums, and records a separate PostgreSQL baseline.

Tables, values, primary/foreign keys, supported defaults/indexes, identity sequence positions, exposure, policies, auth/password hashes, live sessions, encrypted settings and durable job/outbox checkpoints are preserved. Copying does not generate row events. Row counts and canonical content hashes are checked before constraints are validated. Internal backup references point to the copied archive tree; externally stored archives must remain accessible. S3 bytes are a separate recovery asset.

PostgreSQL constraints and representative authorization queries are validated during private conversion and can still block completion after preflight. Only successful completion writes engine.json. A failed conversion removes its private destination; the source databases remain intact. A hard process crash can leave an incomplete destination with engine.migrating.json and without the completion marker; the API refuses to open it: preserve its logs, remove only that reviewed destination, and restart conversion from the unchanged source.

 Activate separately

Review the conversion report and run representative auth, authorized queries, CRUD, realtime, jobs and backup/restore checks against an isolated deployment using the destination. Keep external delivery workers stopped during rehearsal to avoid sending copied pending jobs.

Schedule activation by switching QB_DATA_DIR to the converted directory and starting the new API/worker with the original master key and configuration. Preserve object-store credentials and the same service URLs/origins. Discard old pagination cursors, refetch rows and reconnect subscriptions after activation. Existing SQL scripts must be rewritten for PostgreSQL. Regenerate application types after schema changes; applied SQLite migrations are retained as evidence and are not replayed on PostgreSQL.

Before new writes, rollback can use the retained SQLite directory with the former binary. After accepting writes, returning to SQLite requires reconciliation; engine conversion does not reverse or merge databases.

 Historical backups

Encrypted SQLite archives remain unchanged. Restoring them uses the validated converter and blocks incompatible schemas. Backup restoration retains its existing exclusions/revocations; engine conversion preserves live credentials and durable work. New PGlite datadir archives authenticate their engine version and require a compatible pinned runtime. See [backups and restore](/docs/self-hosting/backups).

title: Monitoring and troubleshooting
text:
Monitoring and troubleshooting

 Health checks

/health indicates process liveness. /ready checks control-database access and reports active owner count. Readiness is not a claim that every external provider is healthy.

 Logs and audit records

Structured API errors include request ID, path, status and a stable code. Audit records include actor, organization/project, action and resource. Credential values, passwords and raw row payloads are not logged by default.

 Terminal display

bun run dev prints a compact startup panel after the API, Studio and Docs respond. It shows service URLs, Bun/PGlite versions, startup duration, the data directory, active-owner limit and worker cadence. A first-owner token file path is shown only while that file exists; token contents remain private. Vite startup banners are suppressed, while frontend warnings/errors remain visible.

QB_LOG_FORMAT=auto uses colored, aligned request logs in development terminals and JSON for production or redirected output. Use QB_LOG_FORMAT=pretty to choose the human display explicitly, or QB_LOG_FORMAT=json for collectors. NO_COLOR disables styling; FORCE_COLOR=1 enables ANSI styling for a compatible renderer. TERM=dumb disables color.

Pretty logs include timestamps, HTTP status, method, path, duration and a shortened request ID. JSON retains the full request ID. Successful, fast job polling is quiet in pretty mode; failures and calls taking at least one second remain visible. Set QB_LOG_INTERNAL=true to show routine polling too. JSON retains these events regardless. Metrics still record every request. Better Auth response statuses are logged as returned, including rejected sign-ins.

Both formats apply the same field allowlist and strip query strings, reset tokens and terminal controls. Do not log request bodies, cookies or credentials through custom console calls. The development launcher keeps its startup panel through hot reload and stops its children together on Ctrl+C.

 Branch unavailable

Inspect provisioning status and confirm the persistent disk is mounted and writable. An unavailable or deadline-terminated owner returns a retriable failure. Restarting the API recovers branch handles; reconcile any uncertain mutation with its idempotency key.

 Busy writers and disk pressure

Requests are bounded by branch queue size and execution deadlines. Monitor database directory sizes and available disk. Stop introducing writes before the disk fills, drain work and follow the backup/restore runbook. Do not delete WAL files to reclaim space from a running database.

 Authentication failures

Verify project key, branch, exact browser origin and application session. A platform session cannot be used as an application identity. Check the selected Resend/SMTP configuration for reset/verification delivery. Provider configuration alone does not prove a social callback works.

 Storage failures

Check S3 endpoint, credentials, physical bucket and bucket MIME/size constraints. Failed upload metadata is not publicly readable. Reconcile pending/deleting objects before retrying remote effects.

 Operational limits

This is a single-node implementation. Do not horizontally scale writable owners without fencing and routing certification. Advanced telemetry, distributed abuse controls and tenant fairness require the release tests listed in the development specification.

 Maintenance and metrics

apps/worker invokes the API's authenticated /internal/maintenance endpoint every minute. It removes expired sessions/idempotency entries, retains the outbox for 24 hours, reconciles abandoned upload/deletion records and creates daily primary-branch snapshots. QB_BACKUP_RETENTION_DAYS defaults to seven. Local workers read .data/worker.token; production injects QB_WORKER_TOKEN.

Scrape /internal/metrics with the worker bearer token from the private network. The gateway returns 404 for internal routes. Prometheus output covers request/error counts, cumulative/max duration, active owners and available disk bytes. Do not interpret these as a complete tracing or performance certification.

 Deployment Doctor foundation

bun run qb doctor --directory . runs read-only redacted inventory without network probes or secret-file reads. Explicit --probe-url https://your-api.example.com performs a bounded readiness GET and refuses redirects/credential-bearing URLs. Exit0: no blocking inventory errors;1: errors;2: invalid invocation. Unknown/unconfigured findings remain visible. S3/mail/push presence is not connectivity or certification; no email or notification is sent.

The private scrape now includes qb_http_request_duration_seconds cumulative latency histograms. Existing counter names remain. Route labels come from declared contracts rather than arbitrary paths, row keys or query values. The full expanded dashboard and alerts remain under development.

 Read the latency histogram

Private Prometheus output adds qb_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{route,le}, _count and _sum. Buckets are cumulative at 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10 and 30 seconds, plus +Inf. Route labels use declared method/path templates; unknown paths aggregate instead of becoming attacker-controlled labels. Existing counters remain compatible.

Expose the scrape only inside the trusted network with the maintenance worker credential. The restricted push principal cannot read metrics or invoke maintenance. Do not embed credentials in URLs, browser examples or telemetry labels. A histogram is not a per-project Operations Dashboard, query tracing or alert service.

See [Deployment Doctor](/docs/self-hosting/doctor) for finding/exit-code interpretation and [Job Inbox](/docs/studio/job-inbox) for experimental private attempt history. Scheduled Studio/email/signed-webhook operational alerts, acknowledgment/deduplication/recovery notifications and advanced owner/outbox/job-health summaries remain under development.

title: Deployment Doctor
text:
Deployment Doctor

 Run local inventory


bun run qb doctor --directory .


From a built CLI installation, use qb doctor --directory checkout-or-application. This inspects runtime/source compatibility and redacted configuration presence. It does not write files, read secret/key contents or load a target dotenv file. If you need checks for a deployment's configuration, securely inject its environment into the invoking process; copying an .env file alone is not evidence that Doctor used it.

 Explicit readiness probe


bun run qb doctor --directory . --probe-url https://api.example.com


Only this option requests network access: a bounded three-second GET to /ready. Supply a bare HTTP(S) origin without credentials, path, query or fragment. Redirects are refused. A successful readiness response is not an S3, mail or push delivery certification.

 Findings and exit codes

The structured report includes inventory and findings with code, severity, status, message and remediation. Checks include pinned runtime/source SDK compatibility, HTTPS/exact origins in production, secret presence, unsafe public secret names, disk capacity/permission observations and S3/mail/push configuration presence.

| Exit | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | No blocking inventory errors. Unknown/unconfigured checks may remain. |
| 1 | Blocking findings need remediation. |
| 2 | Invalid invocation, such as an unsafe probe URL. |

Owner health is reported unknown when it cannot be verified; a lock file is not assumed to prove a healthy owner. Do not interpret unknown or unconfigured findings as passed checks. Reports omit secret values and private paths.

 Current limitations

Live storage probes, test email/push, backup-destination checks and native device configuration certification are not implemented. Doctor never sends a notification, creates an object or changes deployment configuration. These remain [expanded-release requirements](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release). Use [monitoring](/docs/self-hosting/monitoring) and your provider-specific runbook for separately authorized checks.

title: Complete development specification
text:
Complete development specification

Specification version: 1.1 • Date: 6 October 2026 • Product version: 0.1.0

Status: expanded release under development; not a declaration of feature availability.

Precedence: Sections 31–37 define the accepted expanded release and supersede conflicting phase assignments in sections 1–30. Earlier sections retain architectural history and deferred product ideas. The release is incomplete until every expanded requirement has passing acceptance evidence. See [implementation status](/docs/roadmap/expanded-release).

 1. Product definition

QB Flex is a lightweight, self-hostable Backend as a Service for small applications, prototypes, internal tools, and early-stage products. It combines PGlite databases, generated APIs, authentication, realtime, storage, functions, and AI tooling behind a dark monochrome Studio.

The product should offer the convenience of Supabase while using Bun and PGlite as its core. It is a separate platform with its own APIs, SDK, CLI, and security semantics. Supabase interoperability is an explicitly scoped adapter project; neither its CLI nor its PostgreSQL wire protocol works automatically with QB Flex.

Primary goals: provision a project in minutes; create tables visually or through migrations; generate typed REST and GraphQL access; protect every user-facing data path; provide straightforward backups and local development; keep a single-node installation operationally small.

Initial scale assumptions: one writable PGlite database per project branch, local persistent SSD, one active database owner per branch, bounded write workloads, and one primary region. Higher traffic is addressed through independent project placement, read scaling, and quotas rather than simultaneous owners of one database directory.

Terminology: an organization owns projects; a project owns branches; each branch is an isolated database environment. Platform operators and project developers are control-plane identities. Application end users belong to a project authentication realm. A project (organization) role is not an application user role. Application users may be assigned branch-scoped named roles used by Database policies alongside the fixed credential classes anonymous/authenticated/service.

 1.1 Release scope

- P0 — foundation/MVP: organizations, projects, primary branches, PGlite lifecycle, migrations, table editor, generated REST, application RLS, email/password auth, initial social providers, realtime row events, basic S3 storage, TypeScript SDK, CLI, audit logs, backups.
- P1 — complete small-project BaaS: GraphQL, magic links/OTP, 20+ certified social connectors, phone auth, CAPTCHA, webhooks, presence/broadcast/binary channels, resumable uploads, image transforms, snapshot branching, AI inference/vector search, isolated Bun functions, hosted MCP.
- P2 — advanced platform: SSO, OAuth identity provider, read replicas, CDN integration, analytics buckets, RAG workflows, Deno functions, regional placement, Terraform provider, advanced Studio assistant.

These are delivery phases, not removal of requested scope. Feature flags and the Management API must expose availability and experimental status accurately.

 2. Feature coverage and PGlite adaptation

| Requested feature | QB Flex implementation | Phase / qualification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Full PGlite database | PostgreSQL SQL, transactions, indexes, triggers, views, full-text/vector APIs remain planned; owner SQL console | P0; API exposure is a supported subset |
| Auto REST API | Schema registry generates validated CRUD/query routes | P0 |
| Auto GraphQL API | Generated types, relations and mutations using the same query/policy engine | P1 |
| RLS | Default-deny application policy compiler and transaction enforcement | P0; not native PGlite RLS |
| Database webhooks | Transactional event outbox, signed asynchronous delivery | P1 |
| Read replicas | Versioned consistent read-only snapshots first; incremental replication adapter later | P2; eventual consistency |
| Database branching | Consistent snapshot fork plus branch-specific metadata/configuration | P1; no automatic data merge |
| Password, magic link, OTP | Better Auth integration with project-isolated realms and delivery adapters | P0 password; P1 link/OTP |
| Social login, 20+ | Registry of tested OAuth/OIDC provider adapters | P1; credentials/configuration required |
| SSO and phone auth | Enterprise OIDC/SAML adapter and SMS verification adapter | P2 SSO; P1 phone |
| OAuth 2.1 identity provider | Dedicated authorization server configuration and consent UI | P2 |
| CAPTCHA | Pluggable challenge verification on abuse-sensitive endpoints | P1 |
| Postgres change listeners | Native PGlite transaction change stream | P0; optional external Postgres ingestion in P2 |
| Broadcast, presence, binary | Authorized WebSocket channels, heartbeat leases, bounded binary frames | P1 |
| Granular channels | Join/read/write/presence permissions, quotas, retention settings | P1 |
| S3-compatible storage | QB metadata/policies plus S3-compatible object backend | P0 |
| Global CDN | Optional CDN origin adapter; signed private access and public immutable caching | P2; requires CDN infrastructure |
| Image transformations | Isolated Sharp-based processing and derivative cache | P1 |
| Resumable uploads | tus-compatible gateway mapped to multipart object uploads | P1 |
| Analytics buckets | Separate append-only usage/event objects with manifests and scheduled aggregates | P2; not object-store queries by default |
| pgvector embeddings | PGlite extension adapter, not enabled | P1; pgvector requires PostgreSQL |
| Inference, semantic search, RAG | Provider gateway, embedding collections, ingestion jobs and permission-aware retrieval | P1/P2 |
| Ollama, Llamafile | Operator-configured HTTP model adapters | P1; inference runs outside API process |
| OpenAI, LangChain | OpenAI provider adapter and documented LangChain integration | P1 |
| Global TypeScript/Deno functions | Region-pinned isolated Bun workers; optional separate Deno runtime | P1 Bun / P2 Deno; deployment infrastructure required |
| NPM modules | Build-time dependency resolution, lockfiles, runtime-specific compatibility checks | P1 |
| Region pinning | Project placement registry and regional worker routing | P2 |
| Built-in AI API | Unified inference, embeddings and retrieval routes | P1 |
| Supabase CLI | New qb CLI; migration guidance and optional import adapter | P0 CLI; not drop-in compatible |
| Management API | Versioned organization/project/configuration lifecycle API | P0 |
| Terraform provider | Provider over Management API, async operations and drift detection | P2 |
| MCP Server | Hosted Streamable HTTP MCP with scoped browser OAuth | P1 |
| Studio tabs | Database, Auth, APIs, Realtime, Storage, Functions, AI, Logs, Settings | Progressive across phases |

 3. Technical stack and responsibilities

| Layer | Technology | Responsibility |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Toolchain | Bun, TypeScript, Bun workspaces | Runtime, installation, scripts, builds and unit tests |
| Studio | TanStack Start | React application, routes, loaders and server rendering |
| Remote state | TanStack Query | Management requests, job polling, cache invalidation |
| Table UI | TanStack Table | Virtualized database grids, sorting, selection and column controls |
| Forms | TanStack Form | Schema-driven editors and validation |
| UI state | TanStack Store | Project/branch selection, panels and non-server transient state |
| Reactive collections | TanStack DB | Selected Studio collections and live derived queries; not the server database |
| API | Elysia | REST, authentication middleware, WebSocket gateway and management routes |
| GraphQL | GraphQL Yoga candidate mounted under Elysia | Generated schema, execution limits, resolver integration; validate Bun interoperability |
| Persistence | @electric-sql/pglite | Prepared SQL, project databases and control-plane metadata |
| Auth | Better Auth candidate | Password/session/provider mechanisms with explicit tenant isolation |
| UI | ShadCN UI, Tailwind | Accessible primitives and theme tokens |
| UI references | bklit.com, blocks.so, Supabase Library | Selected dashboards, forms and AI UI patterns, adapted to QB branding |
| Object storage | S3-compatible backend | RustFS/S3/R2-style adapter contract, tested per backend |
| Image pipeline | Sharp candidate | Bounded transforms outside request event loop |
| Vector search | PGlite extension candidate; not enabled | Extension-backed similarity search behind interchangeable adapter |
| Telemetry | OpenTelemetry + structured logs | Request traces, metrics and job diagnostics |

Use pinned compatible versions and a committed Bun lockfile. Resolve exact releases during the initial compatibility spike; this document does not prescribe unverified future version numbers. Verify SSR, GraphQL, native extensions, auth adapters and image binaries together on the production Linux image.

TanStack DB is a client reactive collection layer. MVP uses Query for requests; DB collections are introduced only where live joins or optimistic interactions justify them. Cache ownership must be explicit so Query and DB do not independently mutate the same canonical collection.

UI reference libraries are optional copied/adapted components, not mandatory infrastructure dependencies. Confirm component licenses, accessibility, React compatibility, SSR behavior and bundle size before adoption. bklit.com could not be inspected during preparation; treat it as a requested design reference pending review.

 4. Architecture


flowchart TD
  Clients["Studio, SDK, CLI and AI clients"] -- Gateway["TLS gateway and project routing"]
  Gateway -- Control["Management API and platform auth"]
  Gateway -- Data["Project API, auth and realtime"]
  Control -- Catalog["Control PGlite and encrypted config"]
  Data -- Engine["Policy and query engine"]
  Engine -- Owner["Branch database owner"]
  Owner -- PGlite["Branch PGlite and transaction outbox"]
  PGlite -- Jobs["Durable job workers"]
  Data -- Storage["Storage policy gateway"]
  Storage -- Objects["S3 backend"]
  Jobs -- Extensions["Webhooks, AI and isolated functions"]


 4.1 Control plane

Manages organizations, memberships, projects, routing, region placement, branch lifecycle, keys, billing-ready quotas, operations and audit trails. Control-plane credentials never serve as end-user sessions. Initial deployment uses one control PGlite directory with backups; an adapter boundary permits later migration if platform metadata concurrency outgrows PGlite.

 4.2 Data plane

Each branch has its own PGlite directory and its own execution owner. API instances route work to that owner through internal authenticated IPC/RPC. MVP can colocate owner and API; production multi-node deployment must preserve ownership, fencing and authentication. Separate projects can live on different nodes.

Keep database handles in bounded worker processes or Bun workers. WASM SQL execution must not block the shared API event loop. Use queue depth limits, query deadlines, cancellation/worker termination strategy, bounded result streaming and a capped connection cache. Confirm PGlite cancellation support in the selected runtime; if unavailable, terminate isolated query workers and recover safely.

 4.3 Deployment profiles

1. Local: one CLI-managed stack with Studio, API, worker and local S3 backend.
2. Single node: reverse proxy, Studio, API/database owner, jobs and persistent volumes; optional external SMTP, S3 and inference services.
3. Regional: control service plus region-specific owners, functions and storage adapters; each writable branch still has one primary.

Do not mount one WAL database across nodes or network filesystems. Durable local disks plus explicit replication/backup are required. Failover requires old-owner fencing before new-owner activation.

 6. Database lifecycle and supported SQL

 6.1 File layout and settings

Use opaque server-generated IDs and canonical validated paths: /data/projects/project-id/branches/branch-id/main.pglite/. Never derive file paths directly from a user slug. Keep control data outside project files. Authentication and storage metadata use reserved _qb_ tables within the project branch where transactional coordination is needed.

Use @electric-sql/pglite@0.5.10, persistent Node filesystem storage, asynchronous queries/transactions and relaxedDurability: false. One instance serves each database, including its Better Auth Kysely dialect. Transaction callbacks receive the transaction handle; nested domain operations inherit its scope and use savepoints. An OS advisory flock fences the volume and releases on process death. Branch queues remain bounded and query timeouts terminate isolated owners.

Measure memory and cold initialization under the intended branch count. QB_MAX_BRANCH_OWNERS defaults to 4 and accepts 1–32; the ceiling is not a capacity guarantee. Monitor directory size, free disk, owner memory and long queries. Database quotas account for the entire PGlite directory.

 6.2 Exposure contract

Introspect PostgreSQL catalogs for columns, keys, indexes, constraints and migration records. Store exposure metadata separately from physical schema. Tables are private until deliberately exposed with policies. Public CRUD requires stable primary keys; define composite-key encoding. FTS/vector/virtual tables and views require explicit read adapters. Views are private by default because underlying row policies do not automatically apply. Arbitrary triggers, SQL console and migrations are trusted developer operations; they are not available to application users.

Represent booleans as validated 0/1, timestamps as UTC ISO strings or an explicitly selected integer convention, JSON as validated text and blobs as base64 or separate binary endpoints. Return 64-bit integers outside JavaScript's safe range as strings. Document nullability, defaults, generated columns and numeric precision in generated types.

 6.3 Migrations and schema cache

Each migration has ID, checksum, author, applied time, schema version and status. Reject edited applied checksums. Preflight SQL and backup before destructive changes. Apply migrations under an exclusive branch maintenance lock and a PGlite transaction where supported. Table-rebuild migrations copy, validate, swap and regenerate managed triggers atomically. No automatic destructive rollback; restore or apply a forward migration.

After commit, publish a monotonic schema version. Regenerate API metadata, GraphQL schema and type declarations; invalidate prepared statements and realtime/table caches. Requests carry or resolve a coherent schema version. DDL bypassing the migration API is detected and marks the schema stale until reconciled.

 8. Identity, authorization and RLS

 8.1 Credential classes

- Platform session: Studio and organization administration, with owner/admin/developer/viewer roles.
- Publishable project key: identifies project; it does not grant unrestricted data access.
- End-user session/access token: project-bound user identity with validated issuer, audience, expiry and signing key.
- Secret service key: server-only explicitly scoped capability; bypass is opt-in, auditable and prohibited in browser bundles.
- Management token: granular project/org operations; never accepted as an application session.
- MCP OAuth token: tool scopes and selected projects; never inherits unlimited organization access.

Keys support rotation, expiry and revocation. Store hashes of opaque API keys, show plaintext once, rate-limit by credential and never log secrets. For browser sessions use HttpOnly, Secure cookies, controlled SameSite settings and CSRF protections. Bearer SDK sessions must have documented secure storage guidance. CORS origins and auth redirect URLs are per-project allowlists.

 8.2 Policy engine

QB Flex continues to enforce its application policy contracts rather than relying on PostgreSQL native RLS. QB Flex enforces policies at all exposed execution boundaries; trusted direct access to the database file bypasses this layer. Do not market file-level isolation as row authorization.

Policies use a restricted JSON AST, not arbitrary JavaScript or user SQL. Supported expressions include boolean operations, comparisons, null checks, membership and approved relationship existence checks. Claims are verified and server-supplied. Identifiers come from schema allowlists; all values use parameter bindings.

Policy combination rule: default deny; matching permissive policies are ORed, restrictive policies are ANDed, with at least one applicable permissive grant required. Roles are fixed by verified identity or trusted membership resolution.

- SELECT applies USING before filtering, joins, aggregation, counts and pagination.
- INSERT applies WITH CHECK to every prospective row after defaults and before commit.
- UPDATE requires old-row USING and new-row WITH CHECK; protect ownership/tenant columns against unauthorized reassignment.
- DELETE requires old-row USING; event delivery must not leak deleted row content.
- Upsert checks both insert and conflict-update paths. RETURNING obeys readable-column and row permissions.

Writes run inside one owner transaction so authorization and mutation cannot race. Privileged SQL-trigger behavior is treated as trusted schema logic; prevent triggers from rewriting protected values or validate actual final rows before commit. Gate unsupported trigger patterns on exposed tables. Public RPC is limited to reviewed named operations with declared policy context; never expose arbitrary SQL.

GraphQL relations, batched CRUD, realtime, storage, vector retrieval, functions and AI tools must use the same authorization model. Disable public aggregate capabilities that reveal inaccessible rows or hidden columns. A policy test UI evaluates fixtures under explicit simulated identities without minting unrestricted user tokens.

 9. Generated REST API

Base: /v1/projects/{projectId}/branches/{branchId}. SDK resolves a configured branch endpoint; production defaults to an explicit primary alias. No implicit branch from untrusted headers without validation.

| GET /data/{table} | Authorized select, projection, filters, ordering and cursor |

Use keyset pagination with a unique tiebreaker; opaque signed cursors bind filters, identity scope and schema version. Explicitly document that cursors do not establish a cross-request database snapshot. Offset pagination is optional for small Studio grids.

Integrate Better Auth through a project adapter only after proving database and cookie/session isolation. Use a separate platform realm and branch-aware application realm. Implement registration, email verification, login/logout, password reset, session listing/revocation, account linking and optional MFA. Project and branch audiences must be checked on every route.

Magic links and OTPs are single-use, hashed, short-lived and bound to intent. Set resend cooldowns, attempt limits and enumeration-resistant responses. SMS delivery requires an operator-configured provider and spending caps. Phone number changes require verification and sensitive-action reauthentication. Account linking requires verified provider identities and explicit confirmation; email equality alone is insufficient.

 12. Realtime and database change events

 12.1 Commit event source

Install managed INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers on exposed ordinary tables to insert outbox events in the same PGlite transaction. Rollback removes events. Triggers capture primary keys and bounded permitted images; blobs/oversized columns are omitted or referenced. Outbox tables have no recursive capture triggers. Managed trigger regeneration is part of migrations.

Durable consumers poll committed events using a branch-local sequence. At-least-once delivery is expected; event IDs enable deduplication. Transaction IDs preserve grouping; order is defined within one branch, not across projects. Direct trusted SQL changes are captured only on tables with installed triggers. Changes on unsupported virtual tables require explicit adapter events.

This stream replaces the requested PostgreSQL listener for QB-native databases. A future external PostgreSQL connector can ingest logical changes, but is optional and not required to operate PGlite.

 12.2 WebSocket protocol

Endpoint /realtime; versioned envelopes include type, channel, ref, eventId and payload. Operations: join, leave, broadcast, presence-update, database-subscribe, ack and error. Reauthenticate on token refresh/expiry; reevaluate channel membership on revocation or policy changes.

Authorize database events under current identity and policy. Insert/update snapshots require readable new rows. Updates moving a row out of visibility may emit an authorized removal notification containing only previously authorized keys. Delete old images never go to users lacking permission. Replay uses current permissions and schema version; expired cursors return RESYNC_REQUIRED. Clients then query an authorized snapshot and resume with a server-issued cursor boundary to prevent missed changes.

Presence is ephemeral heartbeat state with per-connection IDs, user aggregation, TTL and disconnect grace. Broadcasting is ephemeral by default, acknowledged acceptance does not mean every subscriber received the message. Durable messages belong in application tables.

Default limits: 64 KiB event/frame, heartbeat 25 seconds, lease 75 seconds, 100 joined channels per connection and bounded outbound buffers. Binary frames have an authenticated/versioned header and obey the same channel checks. Slow clients are disconnected with resumable data-event cursors; binary broadcasts have no replay guarantee.

Multi-node fan-out requires an optional broker and shared presence coordination. Until that adapter exists, route branch channels to one realtime owner and advertise single-node semantics.

 13. Database webhooks and durable jobs

Create webhook subscriptions for tables and operations with reviewed payload projection. Queue deliveries only after transaction commit. Sign the exact body using HMAC with timestamp and event ID; publish receiver verification instructions. Support secret rotation with an overlap window.

Delivery policy: bounded exponential backoff with jitter, maximum 10 attempts over 24 hours, per-hook concurrency cap, timeout, dead-letter queue and manual replay. Receivers must deduplicate event IDs. Claim jobs atomically using leases, expire abandoned claims and record attempts. Jobs must be idempotent around external effects.

Block SSRF targets: loopback, link-local, metadata endpoints, private addresses by default, unsupported schemes and redirects to blocked destinations. Revalidate DNS and connection destination. Explicit operator allowlists enable internal targets when required. Redact request credentials and response secrets from logs.

 14. Storage, CDN and uploads

 14.1 Object contract

Buckets have public/private visibility, allowed MIME types, per-object size limits, retention and policies. Store object metadata in PGlite; bytes stay in S3. Object keys are project/branch scoped and normalized. Do not expose raw backend credentials. Authorized upload intents issue short-lived URLs limited to one object, size and content constraints supported by the backend.

Objects transition pending → uploading → verifying → ready or failed. Finalization checks backend existence, expected size/checksum and content validation before publishing metadata. PGlite and S3 are not one atomic transaction: use retryable workflows and orphan cleanup. Deletes use tombstones and retryable backend cleanup. Downloads require ready state and current policy.

 14.2 Resumable uploads

Expose tus-compatible creation, offset reads and chunk writes. Bind upload sessions to user/project/object, authenticate each request and expire abandoned sessions. Adapter maps chunks to S3 multipart uploads with backend minimum part sizes. Persist offsets only after bytes are durable; prevent concurrent offset races. Stream bodies with bounded memory and backpressure. Checksums, resume after restart and multipart abortion are release gates.

 14.3 Transformations and CDN

Transformation API allows bounded width/height, fit, quality and approved formats; rejects arbitrary commands and remote URLs. Detect dimensions before decoding, cap pixel count, strip metadata and use isolated workers with CPU/memory/time limits. Cache derivatives by source version plus canonical transform settings.

Public immutable objects can use long CDN TTLs. Private objects require edge token verification or short-lived signed access whose expiry governs cache behavior. Never share cached private content across users without authorization. Policy revocation and cache purge behavior must be documented; private authorization should be evaluated at delivery for immediate revocation.

Global CDN is an optional provider integration, not a property of PGlite or S3 compatibility. Show CDN provider status, region availability, cache hits and purge failures.

 14.4 Analytics buckets

Store append-only sanitized events as compressed partitioned objects with manifests. Aggregate usage in scheduled jobs into PGlite summaries for Studio. Optional columnar query adapter can be added later. Separate platform usage analytics from application events; define schemas, retention, consent configuration and project-specific access. Do not write sensitive row payloads into usage analytics.

 15. Backups, branches and replicas

 15.1 Backups and restore

Use owner-serialized PGlite datadir exports; never copy a live database directory. Physical snapshots include authenticated engine/version metadata and require the pinned compatible runtime. Snapshot export/import materializes the datadir; archive cryptography streams in bounded chunks. Encrypt backup objects, checksum contents and persist schema/configuration manifests. Proposed defaults: daily full snapshots, 7 daily and 4 weekly copies; retention is operator-configurable.

Restore into a new isolated branch first, run integrity/foreign-key checks and compare expected migration/schema versions. Switching production traffic requires an explicit cutover operation, rollback checkpoint and old-owner fencing. Auth/session and secret restore behavior must be visible. Database snapshots do not restore object bytes unless object-version backups are enabled.

MVP recovery objective target: RPO 24 hours and RTO 60 minutes on the reference dataset, verified by drills. Continuous recoverable replication/backup is a P2 adapter with separately measured objectives. The API outbox alone is not sufficient for point-in-time recovery of every PGlite operation.

 15.2 Branching

Fork creates a consistent database snapshot, new identity/endpoints and independent policies/configuration. Default development branches exclude active sessions, production secrets, webhook destinations and scheduled jobs; auth users are excluded or explicitly sanitized. Storage metadata refers to immutable source objects read-only or copies selected objects through a declared operation. Branch writes always use a separate object prefix.

States: requested, snapshotting, validating, provisioning, ready, failed, deleting. Operations are idempotent and resumable. Branch TTL and disk quotas prevent forgotten copies. Promotion applies reviewed schema migrations to primary; it does not merge arbitrary divergent data. Offer schema diff/export; automatic bidirectional data merge is out of initial scope.

 15.3 Read replicas

P2 baseline replicas are asynchronously refreshed consistent snapshots, reporting applied generation and age. This provides read offload, not low-latency streaming replication. For incremental replicas, choose and certify an PGlite-compatible replication engine before promising latency or automatic failover; do not manually copy live WAL files between running owners.

Clients choose primary or eventual; writes always route to primary. Read-after-write uses primary or waits for a verified consistency token within a timeout. If policy/auth/configuration freshness cannot be guaranteed, route protected reads to primary; stale replicas must not honor revoked access. Region placement and replica residency are explicit. Never allow a read replica to become writable without owner fencing and recovery validation.

 16. AI, vector toolkit and RAG

 16.1 Vector layer

Provide VectorAdapter operations for collection creation, upsert, delete and filtered nearest-neighbor query. The previous sqlite-vec spike is retired. A PGlite-compatible vector extension requires separate packaging, authorization and performance work. Fallback exact search is allowed only for capped small collections and must be labeled. PGlite extension availability does not enable vector product APIs; pgvector integration remains planned.

Collections pin embedding provider/model/version, dimensions, distance metric and normalization. Enforce dimensions and reject mixed models. Index/version changes trigger re-embedding jobs. Store document metadata and ACLs alongside chunks; embeddings link to stable chunk IDs.

Permission filtering must occur before ranking/limit over unauthorized content, or use a bounded authorization-aware search strategy with correctness guarantees. Never fetch unrestricted chunks into a prompt and filter afterward. Delete/revocation must invalidate retrieval caches. Search returns source references, score and embedding version; thresholds are model-specific.

 17. TypeScript and Deno functions

Deploy versioned TypeScript functions with HTTP and async-event triggers. Bun is the default; Deno runs through a separate optional runner. NPM support is evaluated per runtime and dependency; native addons and Node APIs are not universally portable.

Build pipeline: upload source → resolve locked dependencies → isolate build → scan/configuration checks → bundle → hash/store artifact → deploy immutable version → health check → switch alias. No dependency installation on an invocation path. Keep previous versions for rollback.

Run untrusted functions in per-project/version containers with unprivileged UID, read-only root, bounded CPU/memory/time/concurrency, no host filesystem or Docker socket, scoped secrets and controlled egress. A shared JavaScript isolate alone is not sufficient tenant security. For mutually untrusted public tenants, add a hardened sandbox/microVM boundary or keep hosting restricted until isolation is validated.

Proposed defaults: 10-second HTTP execution, 256 MiB memory, 1 MiB request, 5 MiB response and 10 concurrent invocations per project; async workloads use separate limits. Stream responses when supported and stop work on cancellation. User-invoked functions inherit user context by default; privileged service capability must be explicitly assigned and audited.

Region pinning binds function, project database and sensitive storage to permitted regions. Global invocation routes to the pinned region; it does not imply writable databases everywhere. External AI/email providers may process data elsewhere and must be displayed. Scheduled jobs use durable deduplication and at-least-once semantics.

Use optimistic configuration versions to avoid overwriting concurrent changes. List routes use stable cursor pagination. RBAC is enforced per resource; viewer access never includes secrets. Audit creation, rotation, deployment, restore and deletion.

Terraform resources cover project, branch, bucket, policy, auth connection, webhook, function deployment and quota configuration. Data sources expose regions and project metadata.  20. Hosted MCP Server

Expose /mcp using the supported Streamable HTTP protocol and standard tool schemas. Browser OAuth binds client consent to selected organization/projects/branches and explicit scopes. Authorization-code PKCE, resource/audience checks, token expiry and revocation are required. Provide authorization server and protected-resource discovery as required by the pinned MCP protocol version; certify actual ChatGPT/Cursor clients during delivery.

Tools include list_projects, list_tables, describe_table, query_rows, explain_error, generate_types, get_logs, search_docs, create_migration_draft, apply_migration, manage_policy, and deploy_function.  22. Security and isolation requirements

TLS on public and internal remote traffic; scoped internal service authentication; encryption at rest through encrypted volumes and object backend plus encrypted secret envelopes. Stock PGlite is not automatically encrypted. SQLCipher would require a separately certified integration and must not be assumed available in @electric-sql/pglite.

Run API/database/jobs/functions under distinct least-privilege permissions where feasible. Public database files and backend object endpoints are never directly downloadable. Reserved tables and secrets are inaccessible through generated APIs. Disable arbitrary extension loading and ATTACH/PRAGMA operations from untrusted inputs. Install only operator-approved signed/verified extension artifacts.

Enforce per-project CPU/query/write queues, storage, logs, connection, function and inference quotas to control noisy neighbors. Auth endpoints require distributed abuse control before multi-node deployment. Platform administrator MFA, key rotation, incident audit export and dependency scanning are production requirements.

Threat-model gates: cross-project ID substitution, SQL injection, broken policy composition, nested relation leakage, realtime stale authorization, signed URL misuse, branch secret cloning, SSRF, function escape, AI tool privilege escalation and backup exposure. Security tests are release blockers, not optional enhancements.

Purpose/workflows: extend Backups with encrypted off-node S3-compatible destinations, inventory, configured retention, freshness warnings and scheduled isolated restore drills. Database-only success cannot become complete when objects or keys are unverified. No primary alias changes.

Configuration/limits/failure/compatibility: daily snapshots, seven daily/four weekly checkpoints; reference targets RPO24h/RTO60m require measured installation evidence. Configure S3 endpoint/region/bucket/prefix and encrypted credential references separately from normal object storage. Never upload master keys with archives. Bound streams and scratch disk/concurrency; keep legacy restore. Corruption, insufficient disk, missing key/object/destination produce separate actionable report findings; deletion never removes the last required checkpoint accidentally.
